**amd64 runs under emulation** (Rosetta if enabled in Docker Desktop, otherwise QEMU). Expect slower jobs, and some
software (JITs, certain Go/Java/.NET builds) fails under emulation. Prefer arm64 unless a job needs x86_64. amd64 slots
register with an `x64` label instead of `arm64`, and you must rebuild the image after changing `platform`.

### Start at login

kinhin does not start either container runtime, so after a reboot Linux jobs queue until it is running again. Set
it to start at login. On a headless Mac, also turn on automatic login (see
[Keep it running unattended](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/rented-mac.md#keep-it-running-unattended)), because both need a login session.

**apple/container.** `container system start` launches the API server as a launch agent, but it registers that
agent from a plist in the container app data directory, not from `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, so nothing starts it at
the next login. Add your own LaunchAgent. Use the path from `which container` (Homebrew on Apple silicon puts it at
`/opt/homebrew/bin/container`):

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>Label</key>
    <string>local.container-system-start</string>
    <key>ProgramArguments</key>
    <array>
        <string>/opt/homebrew/bin/container</string>
        <string>system</string>
        <string>start</string>
        <string>--disable-kernel-install</string>
    </array>
    <key>RunAtLoad</key>
    <true/>
</dict>
</plist>
```

Save it as `~/Library/LaunchAgents/local.container-system-start.plist`. The `--disable-kernel-install` flag stops the
command from prompting at login, so install the kernel first by running `container system start --enable-kernel-install`
once by hand. To test, log out and back in, then run `container system status`. To remove it, run
`launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/local.container-system-start.plist` and delete the file.

**Docker.** Use the start-at-login setting of your provider:

- **Docker Desktop:** Settings → General → turn on **Start Docker Desktop when you sign in to your computer**
  (off by default).
- **colima:** `brew services start colima` runs colima as a service that starts at login (see the
  [colima FAQ](https://github.com/abiosoft/colima/blob/main/docs/FAQ.md)).
- **OrbStack:** see the [OrbStack documentation](https://docs.orbstack.dev) for its start-at-login setting.

### Tart Linux VMs

Choose **Tart (Linux VM)** under **This Mac → Linux jobs** in the app, or point `base_image:` at a Linux VM. A tart
fleet can serve macOS and Linux VMs at the same time when you use named images with distinct labels — each VM clones
from its own image and advertises only the labels that image is configured with. To make a Linux base VM:

```bash
# from a published image (pick from the menu, or pass --from <ref>)
kinhin image prepare --linux --target <name> --from
# or from an install ISO: creates a bare VM; you install the OS by hand in its window
kinhin image prepare --linux --target <name> --iso <arm64.iso>
# then bake the runner agents into it
kinhin image prepare --source <name> [--target <runner-image>]
```

Guests need an apt-based distro with passwordless `sudo` (the published Cirrus Labs images have both). macOS-only
toolchain entries (Homebrew, CocoaPods) are skipped on Linux guests.

#### Mixing macOS and Linux Tart VMs in one fleet

Give each named image its own distinct labels so jobs select the right OS. A Linux-named image's runners strip the
fleet's `macos` label automatically, so they will not attract macOS jobs:

```yaml
image: "tahoe-base"
labels: [self-hosted, macos, arm64]
images:
  - name: xcode
    base_image: "ghcr.io/cirruslabs/macos-tahoe-xcode:latest"
    labels: [xcode]
  - name: linux
    base_image: "ghcr.io/cirruslabs/ubuntu:latest"
    labels: [linux]
```

Jobs that ask for `[self-hosted, macos, arm64]` run on `image:` (macOS VMs); jobs that ask for `[self-hosted, linux]`
run on the `linux` image (Linux VMs). The fleet `labels:` may still include `macos` — you do not need to remove it.

Runners of the top-level `image:` itself can carry labels too: set top-level `image_labels:`. That is how a Linux
default base answers a label:

```yaml
image: "tahoe-base"
base_image: "ghcr.io/cirruslabs/ubuntu:latest"
labels: [self-hosted, macos, arm64]
image_labels: [linux]
```

A Linux default — whether from `base_image:` or a named image — strips the fleet's `macos` automatically, so macOS
jobs stay on macOS runners. `image_labels:` follows the same rules as a named entry's `labels:` (at least one label
outside the fleet `labels:`, and no label set shared with a named entry); the top-level `warm_pool:` keeps covering
these runners.

## How usage is measured

The app and `kinhin status` show live CPU and RAM per instance (see
[Live CPU and RAM usage](https://github.com/RabinApps/kinhin/blob/v0.0.1-beta-4/docs/app.md#live-cpu-and-ram-usage)). Each runtime is read from the host side:

| Runtime              | Source                                   | CPU                                        | RAM                             |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------- |
| **Tart** (macOS, Linux VMs) | `ps` on the VM's `tart run` process | Percent of one core, from the change in CPU time between samples (can exceed 100%) | Resident memory of that process, against the configured `vm.memory_gb` |
| **Docker**           | `docker stats --no-stream`               | Percent of one core                        | Used / limit                    |
| **apple/container**  | `container stats`                        | Not shown (the CLI only exposes a cumulative counter) | Used / limit         |

For tart these are the host's view of the VM process, not metrics from inside the guest. CPU appears from the second
sample. Samples are cached for about 2 seconds, so several readers (the app, the CLI) share one stats command. Only
active instances are measured.

## Per-repo and per-workflow routing

One fleet can mix runtimes. Add a `runtimes:` section to route by repo, and override per workflow with labels:

```yaml
runtimes:
  default: tart # repos with no route
  budget: { tart: 0.6, appleContainer: 0.4 } # host-budget split; can never overcommit
  routes:
    - pattern: "acme/ios-app" # whole repo → Tart VMs
      runtime: tart
    - pattern: "acme/api" # whole repo → Linux containers
      runtime: appleContainer
    - pattern: "acme/web@Nightly" # one workflow → containers
      runtime: appleContainer
```

Precedence: **workflow route → repo route → `runs-on:` label → default**. Capacity is split by the `budget` weights —
each runtime gets its share of the host's CPU cores and of its RAM, and may only run what both allow — and
`kinhin status` shows the result. If a split would leave a configured route with zero capacity, the app warns you
before you can save it.

Manage routes in **Advanced → Routing** (pools with a live health chip, routes, the default pool, and labels) or with
`kinhin runtimes route add|remove`. The capacity split lives in **Advanced → Capacity**: a budget slider per runtime —
drag it or type a percent, and lock a pool to keep its share fixed while the others rebalance. `kinhin runtimes` prints the same summary. Changes edit only the relevant
part of `config.yaml`, must pass full validation, and reach a running fleet without a restart.

## Route one workflow with the CLI

`kinhin workflow route` moves a single workflow's jobs to a runtime without hand-editing YAML:

```bash
kinhin workflow route ".github/workflows/deploy.yml" appleContainer  # or just the workflow name: "Deploy"
kinhin workflow route ci.yml docker --job build # one job
kinhin workflow route ci.yml tart --dry-run --json # plan only, machine-readable
```

It:

- rewrites each job's `runs-on:` **comment-preservingly** — appending the pool's marker (`kinhin-container`,
  `kinhin-docker`, `kinhin-host`), replacing GitHub-hosted labels the fleet's runners can never satisfy with the
  target pool's exact labels, and stripping stale markers when targeting tart (tart is markerless);
- **reconciles the config route only when precedence requires it** — a repo route that outranks the marker, or a
  markerless target off the default — through the same validated editor `runtimes route add` uses; a running
  daemon reloads it live;
- refuses what it can't safely edit (<code v-pre>${{ … }}</code> expressions, `{group:, labels:}` mappings, reusable-workflow jobs)
  and points at `kinhin runtimes route add <owner/repo>@<Workflow> <runtime>` for those;
- refuses a runtime whose pool isn't configured, printing its setup commands and [the comparison above](#choosing-a-linux-runtime).

`--consent` is required for `host`, and `kinhin runtimes --json` reports the per-runtime `availability` sweep
(`ready` / `missing:<tool>` / `broken:<reason>`), so scripts can pick a runtime this Mac can actually run.

## Windows (not available as a local runtime on Mac)

Windows CI jobs cannot run locally on a Mac through kinhin's container runtimes, and **Windows containers are not an option on macOS at all**.

- **`microsoft/windows` / `mcr.microsoft.com/windows` are Windows Server containers.** They share the Windows NT kernel with the host and need a Windows host kernel (and, for process isolation, a matching host build). Docker Desktop on macOS runs a Linux VM and has no Windows container mode, so it cannot pull or run these images. There is no way to switch Docker Desktop on a Mac into Windows-container mode.
- **"Windows in a container" projects (e.g. `dockur/windows`) are not Windows containers.** They are full VMs (QEMU/KVM) packaged to run inside a Linux Docker container, using `/dev/kvm` from the Linux host. Docker Desktop on macOS does not expose `/dev/kvm` to containers, and Apple's `container` CLI is a microVM runtime — not a KVM host — so neither can run these. Macs also have no Linux KVM to pass down in the first place. Even where KVM is available, the result is a full Windows VM, not a lightweight Windows container.

**If you need Windows CI on a Mac fleet, the realistic local path is a Windows VM on Apple Silicon**, driven by kinhin as a fleet runtime — see [Windows VMs on Apple Silicon](https://github.com/RabinApps/kinhin/blob/main/docs/plans/windows-vms-apple-silicon.md). That plan is substrate-probed and not yet implemented; the gating question is a bootable Windows ARM guest source (Parallels template/ISO, or a scripted hypervisor backend) and the per-forge Windows runner install/registration story.

**If you do not need to run Windows locally**, route Windows jobs to GitHub-hosted Windows runners instead. GitHub Actions now has Windows ARM64 hosted runners (`windows-11-arm` label, public repositories) and standard Windows hosted runners — add the appropriate `runs-on` label and kinhin's fleet (macOS + Linux) stays where it is.

## Host mode: run jobs directly on your Mac

Host mode runs a job as an ephemeral runner process **on your Mac itself**: no VM, no container. It's fast and sees
your real toolchains, but has **no isolation**: the job runs with your user's privileges and can read your files and
reach your network. Use it only for repositories you fully trust, never a public repo that accepts pull requests from
strangers.

It is opt-in per route and needs explicit consent:

```yaml
runtimes:
  default: tart # `default: host` is rejected; host is never a fallback
  routes:
    - pattern: "acme/scripts"
      runtime: host
      consent: true # required for host routes
```

- **Consent is enforced everywhere.** Config validation, `kinhin runtimes route add <pattern> host --consent`, and the
  app's Add Route sheet all refuse without it. Host routes show an _unisolated_ warning in the route list.
- **Install the agent once.** Run `kinhin setup repair host-agent` (or use the one-click fix in the setup checklist). The
  runners are installed, SHA-256 verified, under `~/Library/Application Support/Kinhin/host-runner`.
- **Workflows can opt in** with `runs-on: [kinhin-host]`. Only opted-in workflows can ever land on your Mac.
- **The machine isn't reset between jobs.** Each runner is ephemeral and gets a work directory that is scrubbed
  afterwards, but anything a job installs outside it persists.
- Host routes work for GitHub, Gitea, Forgejo and GitLab (the last three run live in the e2e suite).

---

Source: https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/scaling.md

# How scaling works

The capacity cap, the scaling loop, job density, and how kinhin recovers from restarts.

[← Back to README](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/index.md) · Why this exists: [Why kinhin](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/why-kinhin.md)

## Capacity

The effective concurrency cap is
`min(max_runners, (cores − reserve.cpu) / vm.cpu, (RAM − reserve.memory_gb) / vm.memory_gb, free_disk / disk_per_vm)` —
`disk_per_vm` is your `disk_gb` when set, else a runtime default (50 GB for Tart VMs, 8 GB for
Linux container slots). The scaler re-checks free disk before every spawn and holds new VMs when
the disk would dip below `reserve.disk_gb` plus one instance's footprint — a queue burst can
never fill your disk. `kinhin doctor` prints the cap and the binding constraint, and warns under
the same rule before the fleet reaches it: `WARNING: disk pressure` (the guard itself is the
`diskPressure` field of `doctor --json`), stating how much the images hold and what
`kinhin image prune` would reclaim.
Not sure how big a Mac you need? See [Hardware requirements & sizing](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/hardware.md).

When several runtimes are configured, this budget is partitioned across their pools by the
`runtimes.budget` weights — for CPU cores and for RAM separately, so a light-on-cores yet fat-in-memory runtime is
bounded by its RAM share too (see [Runtimes](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/runtimes.md#per-repo-and-per-workflow-routing)). The default pool gets
whatever share the others leave.

## The scaling loop

Every `poll_interval` seconds the engine:

1. Cleans up any failed instances from the previous pass.
2. Asks each forge for queued jobs on its scope and filters them by `labels`.
3. **Routes** each job to a runtime — workflow route → repo route → `runs-on:` label → default —
   and buckets the demand per pool.
4. Computes the desired instance count **per pool**:
   `desired = clamp(ceil(pool_queue / runners_per_vm), min_runners, pool_cap)`, where `pool_cap`
   is that runtime's slice of the host budget (`budget` weights, applied to cores and RAM alike) when multiple runtimes are
   configured, or the full [capacity cap](#capacity) for a single-pool fleet.
5. Spawns instances up to `desired` (linked clone → boot → SSH → register `runners_per_vm`
   runners → `run.sh`) — Tart VMs for macOS pools and for Tart Linux VMs, apple containers or
   Docker slots for the container Linux pools (see [Choosing a Linux runtime](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/runtimes.md#choosing-a-linux-runtime)),
   and a runner process on the Mac itself for host routes.
6. Deletes idle instances when `desired` drops (scale to zero by default).

When starts keep failing.

If a runtime's instances fail to register twice in a row (a bad image, a runner
that exits at once), kinhin stops respawning them in a loop: that runtime waits 30 s, then 1 min, 2 min … up to
10 min before the next attempt, other runtimes keep going, and the status line shows `runner starts failing on
<reason> … retrying in Ns: </reason>` with the runner's own output. One successful registration clears it. A job
cancelled on GitHub before a runner picks it up is not a failure: the idle instance is simply removed
(`cancelled remotely` in the log).

### Poll cadence

`poll_interval` is the normal cadence. Two things stretch it:

- **Idle.** After 5 minutes with no queued jobs and no instances, kinhin polls every 60s (or `poll_interval`, if
  longer). The first new job restores the normal cadence. The 5-minute grace keeps multi-stage workflows fast, because
  the fleet is briefly empty between `needs:` stages.
- **API budget.** kinhin reads GitHub's rate-limit headers. Below 25% of the hourly budget it polls half as often, and
  below 10% a quarter as often. When the budget is exhausted it waits for the reset (at most 15 minutes). The status
  line notes any slowdown, for example `queue age: 12s old · checking every 60s (idle)`.

GitHub reads are conditional, so a poll that finds nothing changed gets a 304, which doesn't count against the rate
limit.

## Warm pool

`warm_pool: N` keeps `N` Tart VMs cloned, booted and SSH-ready but **not registered** with any forge. When a job
arrives, the scaler claims a warm VM, binds it to the account that has the demand, and runs only the registration step,
so the job skips `tart clone` and boot. With the default `0` the feature is off.

Each Tart image has its own pool. The top-level `warm_pool` covers `image:`, and `warm_pool` on an
[`images:` entry](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/runtimes.md#multiple-macos-images) covers that image, so an Xcode image can stay warm while the base
stays cold, or the other way round.

- Warm VMs take slots under `max_runners` and count against the capacity cap, including Apple's limit of two macOS VMs
  per Mac. They are evicted when a job needs the slot, so a warm VM never delays work that a cold start could serve.
- The pool tops up only when nothing is queued and `min_runners` is met. In ephemeral mode the replacement for a
  finished VM is started on the next pass, so the poll interval applies.
- A job claims a warm VM of the image it runs on. Jobs routed to a per-project image (`projects:`), and the other
  runtimes, start cold.
- A named image that was never prepared gets no warm VMs. Its `warm_pool` is skipped, with a log line, until it exists. Kinhin reads `tart list` at most once a minute, so an
  image prepared while the fleet runs starts its warm pool within a minute.
- The base `warm_pool` and every entry's `warm_pool` together must fit in `max_runners`.
- A warm VM older than `warm_max_age_minutes` (default 60) is recycled, and so is one whose pool is turned off or whose
  `images:` entry was removed. After a restart, warm VMs are re-checked rather
  than trusted.

This differs from `min_runners`, which keeps *registered* idle runners on the forge.

## Healing

The scaling loop recovers from most failures by itself: the spawn backoff above, teardown retries, forge re-attach
backoff, and an orphan sweep for instances kinhin started but has no record of (see [Restarts](#restarts)). The [healing agent](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/healing.md) runs in its
own loop beside it and covers what those do not, without ever delaying a scaling pass:

- **Warm VMs.** A warm VM waits with nothing driving it, so no liveness watch sees it die. The engine's orphan sweep
  (every 2 minutes, healing on or off) lists each runtime once and removes the record of a warm VM deleted or stopped
  outside kinhin, so it stops holding a slot and the pool tops up again; the healing journal notes each removal.
- **Disk pressure.** When the disk guard holds spawns, the agent prunes the toolchain cache (with `auto_prune` on) and
  then asks before pruning unused images.
- **Spawn backoff.** The backoff keeps a failing runtime from respawning in a loop; the agent looks at why. A stopped
  Apple container system is started on its own; a missing runtime or a broken tart waits for your approval.
- **Detached accounts.** An account that dropped off for a minute is re-attached at once instead of waiting out its
  backoff; a rejected token is shown to you.

With `healing.enabled: false` all of the engine's own retries still run. `kinhin heal` shows what the agent did.

## Restarts

When the daemon or app restarts, kinhin reads its saved state (`fleet.json` in the state directory) and checks what is still
running on each runtime before it starts anything new.

- **Intact `fleet.json`.** Records are reloaded. A runner that was registered (idle or busy) is watched, not registered again,
  so its job is not disturbed. The exception is an idle classic (non-ephemeral) runner in an Apple container or Docker
  container: the agent dies with a stopped container, so when the forge lists runners and has none for it, it is registered
  again. A warm VM returns to the warm pool.
- **Unreadable `fleet.json`.** kinhin moves the file aside to `fleet.json.corrupt-<timestamp>` (it is never overwritten), and
  the status alert and `kinhin status` name the kept copy. The engine starts with no VM records, so job and repo attribution
  is lost. It then re-adopts each VM it finds and checks that VM's runner with the forge, asking each account once:
  - a runner the forge still has (busy or idle) is **watched, not registered again**, so a running job is not disturbed;
  - a VM with no runner on the forge is registered as normal;
  - a VM whose forge cannot be asked is **held** and not registered until it can be (shown by the `adoption` status alert).

  Beta 2 registered every re-adopted VM again, which could fail a running job (see the known issue in
  [GitHub forge notes](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/forges/github.md)). The fix shipped in beta 3; on beta 2, restart only when no jobs are running.
- **Unlisted runtime.** If a runtime can't be listed (Tart wedged, a daemon down), its records are kept, and nothing is removed
  on a failed listing.
- **Orphan sweep.** Only an instance with no record, under a name kinhin generates, is removed, and only after it stays
  unclaimed for ten minutes (`orphanGrace`). An instance the restart re-adopted has a record, so the sweep does not remove it.
- **Warm VMs after an unreadable `fleet.json`.** The pool flag is lost, so a re-adopted warm VM comes back as an ordinary runner.
  It counts against `max_runners` until scale-down removes it.
- **Forges with no runner list.** Some servers (Gitea before 1.24, Forgejo, Bitbucket) cannot say which runner belongs to which
  VM. With nothing running in the account's scope, a re-adopted VM is registered. With a job running, it is watched as busy, and
  it is removed once the scope goes quiet.
- **Partly registered VMs.** With `runners_per_vm` above 1, a VM can have only some of its runners on the forge. If none of them
  is busy, the set is registered again. If one is busy, the VM is watched. The missing runner never appears, so the VM is removed
  only at the watch deadline (up to 6 hours). This is a known limit.
- **Accounts without a forge.** A VM whose account is still configured but has no forge attached is held, with the `adoption`
  status alert, and removed after one hour. A VM whose account was removed from the config is released at once.

## Pausing and auto-resume

A paused fleet doesn't spawn new instances. With `auto_resume: true` it keeps watching the queue while paused and
resumes itself once the queue is empty. This is what makes a deliberate pause safe, for example the Shortcuts "Delete
VM" action pauses first so autoscaling can't recreate what you just deleted. If every forge fetch fails while paused,
the engine stays paused rather than treat silence as "nothing to do".

Every status surface (menu bar, Fleet tab, `kinhin status`, Siri) shows how old the queue numbers are, so a paused
snapshot never looks fresh during an outage. `kinhin status --json` exposes `paused`, `autoResume`, `pollInterval` and
`queueAgeSeconds`.

## Job density

`runners_per_vm` is the density knob: with the default `1`, each job gets its own VM (most
isolation); with `4`, one VM serves four concurrent jobs before the scaler spawns another. Small
jobs on identical macOS stacks are the sweet spot — set it high enough that `vm.cpu`/`vm.memory_gb`
cover the _sum_ of the jobs you expect on one VM.

With a GitHub scale set (`scale_set:`), keep `runners_per_vm: 1`: GitHub does not hand a second job to another idle
runner in the same VM, and the scaler counts those slots as capacity, so the job waits for the first one to finish
([details](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/forges/github.md#a-second-job-stays-queued-while-the-vm-has-idle-runners-runners-per-vm-1)).

## Running on multiple Macs

Each Mac runs its own engine and polls the forge independently; kinhin does not coordinate between
machines (the daemon lock only guards against two daemons on the _same_ Mac). If two Macs serve the
same repo with the same labels, both see a queued job and both spawn a runner for it. The forge
hands the job to exactly one of them, so it never runs twice, but the other Mac boots a VM it didn't
need.

To keep demand from overlapping, give each Mac its own label:

```yaml
# Mac A
labels: ["mac-a"]
```

```yaml
# Mac B
labels: ["mac-b"]
```

A workflow then picks the Mac it wants:

```yaml
runs-on: [self-hosted, macos, arm64, mac-a] # only Mac A spawns for this job
```

A job counts as demand only when it requests _every_ configured label, so the other Mac ignores it.
To fan one job across both Macs, use a matrix:

```yaml
strategy:
  matrix:
    mac: [mac-a, mac-b]
runs-on: [self-hosted, macos, arm64, "${{ matrix.mac }}"]
```

Things to know:

- A job with neither label matches no Mac and stays queued.
- A shared pool (the same labels on both Macs) still works, but a burst can make both Macs spawn.
  Lower `max_runners` on the weaker Mac to limit the waste.

### Requeue and skip

From the Fleet tab, the **Requeue** and **Skip** buttons in the _Requeue / skip queued_
section cancel or drop the queue's matching jobs. Org-scope forges re-queue/skip the
fleet-wide queue; repo-scope forges act on that one forge. Both are single-command
actions behind the same pending-state and AlertKit failure handling as Start/Stop.

See [Requeue and skip queued jobs](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/requeue-skip.md) for the full behavior.

---

Source: https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/toolchains.md

# Toolchains & the shared cache

How to get Go, Node, Xcode, Flutter and friends onto kinhin runners, and how to cache their downloads.

[← Back to README](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/index.md)

Every job runs on a fresh clone of an image, so anything a job installs is thrown away with the VM. There are three
ways to get tools onto a runner:

| Approach | Best for | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Base image](#bake-tools-into-the-base-image) | Tools every job on this Mac needs | A provision script run by `kinhin image prepare` |
| [Per project](#per-project-toolchains) | Different repos needing different versions | `.kinhin/config.yml` in the repo, or `projects:` in `config.yaml`. kinhin bakes an image per project. |
| [Per job](#per-job-toolchains) | Tools only some workflows need, and all Linux container runtimes | `kinhin-toolchain install` in a workflow step |

For store releases with fastlane (iOS, Android, Flutter, React Native, Expo), see [Mobile releases with fastlane](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane.md).

Per-job installs also work with the usual `actions/setup-go`, `actions/setup-java` and friends, at the cost of
downloading the toolchain in every job. The [shared cache](#the-shared-download-cache) removes most of that cost.

## Bake tools into the base image

`kinhin image prepare` can run **your provision script** inside the VM once, after the runner agents are installed.
Every runner then boots with whatever the script installed. The script runs as the `admin` user, and a failure aborts
the prepare and leaves the previous image intact.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# ~/kinhin/provision.sh
brew install wget cmake
mise install go@1.23.4 rust@1.82 java@temurin-21   # exact versions; mise ships in the base image
go version && rustc --version && java -version      # output is logged in `kinhin logs` as an audit trail
```

Wire it up with a flag (wins) or the config key:

```bash
kinhin image prepare --provision-script ~/kinhin/provision.sh
```

```yaml
# config.yaml
provision_script: "~/kinhin/provision.sh"
```

- **The script is your version pin.** Every prepare rebuilds from the pristine upstream image, so edit the script and
  re-run prepare to change toolchains. Homebrew and mise are both in the base image.
- **Need full Xcode?** Don't install it from a script (tens of GB). Point `image:` (or `image prepare --source`) at
  Cirrus Labs' `macos-tahoe-xcode:16`, `macos-golden-gate-xcode` or `macos-runner:tahoe` images instead.
- The script has its own 30-minute budget. A configured script that is missing or empty fails the setup checklist
  before a long prepare starts.

## Per-project toolchains

Declare what a project needs and kinhin installs, pins and verifies it. Each distinct set is baked into its own
**derived image** (Tart only), so repos with different versions never interfere. Toolchains are always per project;
there is no global list.

You can declare them in two places:

```yaml
# config.yaml: you choose
projects:
  - pattern: "acme/api"                  # owner/name, or owner/* for every repo of an owner
    toolchains:
      specs: ["go@1.23.4", "node@22", "uv"]
      brew: ["wget", "cmake"]
      stacks: ["flutter@3.24.0"]
```

```yaml
# .kinhin/config.yml in the repo: the repo chooses (needs repo_file: true on its projects: entry)
toolchains:
  specs: ["go@1.23.4", "node@22", "pnpm"]
```

Jobs from a repo with neither run on the plain base image.

### The `.kinhin/config.yml` file

Put it at `.kinhin/config.yml`. The older `.kinhin.yml` at the repo root is still read when `.kinhin/config.yml` is absent; if both exist, `.kinhin/config.yml` wins. The same `.kinhin/` folder can hold other kinhin files for the repo, such as the [video configs](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/video-config.md) in `.kinhin/videos/`, which this loader never reads.

kinhin reads the file **at the ref the job runs at**, so a `release/1.x` branch can pin `go@1.22.5` while `main` pins
`go@1.23.4`. The file is opt-in: it is ignored unless the matching `projects:` entry sets `repo_file: true`. It is
deliberately limited, because it is untrusted input that decides what gets installed on your Mac:

- Only a `toolchains:` section with `specs` and `stacks` is accepted. No `brew`, `provision_script`, `base_image` or
  cache settings.
- Every spec must be in the [curated catalog](#the-catalog). Unknown mise backends (`ubi:`, `npm:`, `cargo:`) are
  rejected. (Specs in `config.yaml` may fall through to mise.)
- The file is capped at 16 KB. A missing, invalid or oversize file is logged, shown in Diagnostics, and treated as
  absent. It never blocks the fleet.
- Fork pull requests never use the repo file. See [Security](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/security.md#per-project-toolchains).

GitHub, Gitea/Forgejo and GitLab supply the ref and the file.

### Generating toolchains

`kinhin toolchains detect` scans a local checkout and writes the `toolchains:` block for you, with the evidence behind
every pick.

```bash
kinhin toolchains detect                  # scan the current directory
kinhin toolchains detect ~/code/acme-web  # or another checkout
kinhin toolchains detect --write          # write <path>/.kinhin/config.yml (refuses to overwrite)
kinhin toolchains detect --write --force  # overwrite an existing file
kinhin toolchains detect --json           # machine-readable result only
```

**stdout carries the `.kinhin/config.yml` block**, so it pipes cleanly. The evidence table and anything kinhin couldn't map go
to **stderr**. For a Node repo with a pnpm lockfile and TypeScript:

```text
$ kinhin toolchains detect ~/code/acme-web > .kinhin/config.yml
  node@20       .nvmrc: .nvmrc pins node v22.1.0
  node@20       package.json: engines.node >=20
  playwright    .github/workflows/ci.yml: runs `playwright`
  pnpm@9.1.0    package.json: packageManager pnpm@9.1.0
  typescript    package.json: depends on typescript
not in the catalog (skipped): husky

$ cat .kinhin/config.yml
toolchains:
  specs: ["node@20", "pnpm@9.1.0", "playwright", "typescript"]
```

Paste the same block under a `projects:` entry in `config.yaml` if you'd rather not commit a repo file.

`--json` prints only `{ specs, stacks, evidence, unmatched, recommendations }`. `--write` saves the block as `<path>/.kinhin/config.yml` (creating the folder) and
refuses to replace an existing file unless you add `--force`.

**What it reads:**

- **Version files:** `.tool-versions`, `mise.toml`, `.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, `.python-version`, `.ruby-version`,
  `.go-version`, `.java-version`, `.swift-version`.
- **Manifests and lockfiles:** `package.json` (`engines`, `packageManager`, `devDependencies`), npm/pnpm/yarn/bun
  lockfiles, `go.mod`, `Cargo.toml`, `rust-toolchain`, `pyproject.toml`, `requirements.txt`, `uv.lock`, `Gemfile`,
  fastlane, `pubspec.yaml`, `Package.swift`, Gradle and Maven files, `composer.json`, `.csproj` (also one folder down when it sets `UseMaui`), `global.json`,
  `mix.exs`, `deno.json`, `Dockerfile`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `Justfile`, `Taskfile`, `*.tf`, `Chart.yaml`, Expo and React
  Native projects, `vercel.json`, `wrangler.toml`.
- **GitHub Actions:** `.github/workflows/*` `setup-*` actions and known CLIs called in `run:` lines.

**Precedence.** For a version, a version file beats a manifest, a manifest beats a workflow, and a workflow beats the
catalog's default spec. Ranges are reduced to their floor: the major version for node, java, bun and deno (`^20.1` and `>=20` both become `20`), major.minor for the rest (`>=3.11,<4` becomes `3.11`).

**Your project's own versions.** Every tool the catalog can pin gets the version the project already uses, never a newer
default. Besides the version files and workflows above, that means the `go.mod` `toolchain`/`go` lines, `rust-version`,
`Pipfile`/`runtime.txt`, `mix.exs`, Terraform `required_version`, the Gradle and Maven wrappers, JDK levels from Gradle
and `pom.xml`, the Kotlin plugin, `.fvmrc` and `pubspec.yaml` for Flutter and Dart, `package.json` `volta` and the
version ranges of npm tools such as TypeScript or ESLint. A tool whose project states no version falls back to the
catalog default. `php`, `composer`, `dotnet`, `yamllint` and the Homebrew-only cloud CLIs take no `@version` in the
catalog, so they are emitted bare.

**Always valid.** Runtimes are added automatically where the catalog requires them (pnpm or `vercel` pull in `node`;
`kotlin` or `gradle` pull in `java`), so the output satisfies the [no-implicit-installs rule](#rules-that-apply-to-every-declaration).
Only [catalog](#the-catalog) tools and stacks are emitted; anything else is listed as unmatched, because a repo file
cannot use `npm:` or `ubi:` specs. The block is checked by the same loader the engine uses and stays within the 16 KB
cap, so kinhin never emits YAML it would reject.

**Xcode and Swift.** Full Xcode is too large to install from a script, so it is never a toolchain. When the scan sees an
`.xcodeproj` or `.xcworkspace` (also under `ios/` and `macos/`), a `.xcode-version`, a `Package.swift` that targets iOS,
tvOS, watchOS or visionOS, or a workflow that calls `xcodebuild`, it prints a **recommendation** (stderr, and the
`recommendations` field in `--json`) to set `base_image:` (or `image prepare --source`) to an image that includes Xcode,
such as `ghcr.io/cirruslabs/macos-tahoe-xcode:latest`, and leaves `swift` out of the block because Xcode ships its own.
A plain Swift package (macOS-only or no Apple-platform targets, built with `swift build`) gets the `swift` toolchain
instead and no recommendation. Its version comes from `.swift-version`, else the `// swift-tools-version:` line in
`Package.swift`, else a workflow's `swift-version`, else `latest`.

**Limits.** It scans a local directory only (no remote repos), reads GitHub Actions workflows only (no GitLab or Gitea
CI files), and doesn't edit `projects:` entries in `config.yaml`. The result is a starting point: review it, and remember
the file is only honored when the `projects:` entry sets `repo_file: true`.

### Resolution order

For each job, the first level that yields toolchains wins:

1. The repo's `.kinhin/config.yml` (or older `.kinhin.yml`) at the job's ref (only if `repo_file: true`). A fork's PR, or a job whose forge does not say whether it is a fork's (GitHub scale-set, Gitea and Forgejo), reads it from the default branch instead.
2. The matching `projects:` entry's own `toolchains:`.
3. Nothing: the plain base image.

### The `projects:` keys

| Key           | Meaning |
| ------------- | ------- |
| `pattern`     | Required. `owner/name` or `owner/*`, case-insensitive, unique. |
| `repo_file`   | Honor the repo's `.kinhin/config.yml` (default `false`). |
| `toolchains`  | `specs`, `brew` and `stacks` for matching repos with no usable repo file. |
| `share_cache` | Mount the [shared download cache](#the-shared-download-cache) for this project (default `false`; always off for fork PRs and jobs of unknown origin, which includes every GitHub scale-set, Gitea and Forgejo job). |

Changes to `projects:` apply to a running fleet without a restart.

### Rules that apply to every declaration

- **Nothing is installed implicitly.** A stack that needs a runtime (`vercel` needs node) is a validation error that
  names the fix, until you list the runtime too.
- **Verification is the audit trail.** Each tool carries a verify command (`go version`, `flutter --version`, …). A
  bake aborts with the previous image intact if a check fails.
- **Deploy credentials stay per job.** Pass `VERCEL_TOKEN` and cloud credentials with workflow `env:`; they are never
  baked into an image.
- Versions may only contain `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ + -`.

### The catalog

Run `kinhin toolchains` for the full list. Everything installs on macOS and Linux images unless noted.

- **Languages & runtimes:** node, go, rust, python, ruby, java, bun, deno, uv, zig, erlang, elixir, kotlin, scala,
  clojure, dart, swift, lua, julia, php, dotnet. (kotlin, scala and clojure need `java` selected too.)
- **JavaScript tools** (need node): pnpm, yarn, playwright, cypress, netlify-cli, firebase-tools, typescript, eslint,
  prettier, turbo, nx.
- **Build & quality:** cmake, ninja, maven, gradle, sbt, just, task, jq, yq, direnv, shellcheck, hadolint, yamllint,
  composer, fastlane.
- **Cloud & DevOps:** terraform, opentofu, kubectl, helm, kustomize, k9s, pulumi, packer, vault, gh, awscli, gcloud,
  flyctl, supabase.

**Stacks** bundle several pieces:

- `flutter[@version]`: Flutter SDK (default `stable`), plus fvm and CocoaPods on macOS. On Linux it builds web and
  Linux desktop out of the box; Android needs `java` and an Android SDK you provide, and iOS needs macOS.
- `expo[@version]`: `eas-cli` (needs node).
- `react-native`: watchman, CocoaPods and JDK 17 (macOS). Add node yourself if you build JS.
- `vercel[@version]` and `cloudflare[@version]`: the `vercel` and `wrangler` CLIs (need node).

### Derived images

- **Naming.** Derived images are named `<base image>-p<8 hex>`. Two repos that resolve to the same set share one image.
  Rebuilding the base image changes the digest, so derived images are rebaked.
- **Baking.** `kinhin image prepare --project owner/name [--ref X]` bakes one ahead of time. Otherwise the first job
  that needs a set starts the bake, and that job (and any queued behind it) runs on the base image until it's ready.
- **Pruning.** The number of derived images is capped by `max_project_images` (default 8) with least-recently-used
  eviction. `kinhin toolchains prune` and `kinhin cleanup` remove them too. The base image and running VMs are never
  touched.
- **Disk.** A derived image is a copy-on-write clone, so it costs roughly the toolchain itself: a few GB, and 5 GB or
  more for Flutter. `tart list` and `du` over-report because they count shared blocks once per image.
- **Linux runtimes.** apple/container and Docker get no derived images; use [per-job installs](#per-job-toolchains).

Useful commands:

```bash
kinhin toolchains --project owner/name [--ref main]     # what a repo resolves to
kinhin image prepare --project owner/name [--ref main]  # bake its image now
kinhin toolchains list-images                           # derived images: size, last used
kinhin toolchains prune [--dry-run]
kinhin image list                                  # derived images alongside every other installed image
kinhin image delete <name> [--yes]                  # delete one by name (reports unless --yes)
kinhin image prune [--yes]                          # one pass: stale records + unused local images
```

The app's **Advanced → Toolchains** tab shows the same information read-only: your `projects:` rules with their
images (size, last used, delete, rebuild), the catalog, and copyable `.kinhin/config.yml` examples.

## Per-job toolchains

Every prepared image carries `kinhin-toolchain`, a helper that installs catalog tools from a workflow step. It is the
only way to get toolchains on the apple/container and Docker runtimes.

```yaml
jobs:
  web:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, kinhin]
    steps:
      - run: kinhin-toolchain install node@22 pnpm playwright
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pnpm install && pnpm test
```

- It runs the same install and verify steps as a bake, so a failed install fails the step. Unknown ids fall through to
  `mise use --global`.
- Later steps see the tools: new `PATH` entries go to `$GITHUB_PATH` and `$GITHUB_ENV` (GitHub and Gitea runners).
- Runtimes install first. A tool whose runtime you didn't list fails with the command to fix it.
- Pair it with `share_cache: true` so repeat installs are mostly cache hits.
- `kinhin-toolchain list` shows the available ids. `kinhin toolchains helper [--linux]` prints the helper for audit.

Bundlers like Vite, Next.js and Turbopack are project dependencies: they come from `node_modules` via `npm ci`, not
from the image. The image provides node, `corepack enable` (so `packageManager` picks pnpm or yarn), and warm package
caches.

## The shared download cache

A host-side cache at `~/Library/Application Support/Kinhin/toolchain-cache/` lets repeated bakes and installs skip
re-downloading mise tools, Homebrew bottles, npm packages, Flutter SDKs, Go modules, Gradle, NuGet and browsers.
Turn it on per project:

```yaml
projects:
  - pattern: "acme/api"
    share_cache: true
```

The cache is mounted into that project's bakes and runners, in a subdirectory scoped to the project. It is off by
default and always off for fork PRs and jobs of unknown origin (GitHub scale-set, Gitea and Forgejo jobs). On Linux container runtimes it is bind-mounted at `/var/kinhin-cache`.

> **Don't enable it for untrusted code.** The cache is writable and holds things later jobs _execute_ (Cargo's `bin/`,
> Flutter SDKs, Playwright browsers, Gradle init scripts). A fork PR could plant a binary there that a later job runs,
> and the next bake could carry it into an image. Per-project subdirectories keep repos from poisoning each other, but
> leave `share_cache` off on a fleet that runs outside contributors' PRs.

### Expiry and pruning

The cache expires entries unused for 30 days and evicts least-recently-used entries beyond 50 GB. A one-hour grace
window means a prune never races a live download. Pruning only touches this regenerable cache, never images or running
VMs.

```yaml
# config.yaml
toolchain_cache:
  auto_prune: true   # after each bake, and daily while the fleet runs (default true)
  max_age_days: 30   # 0 = never expire (default 30)
  max_gb: 50         # 0 = unlimited (default 50)
max_project_images: 8
```

Sweep by hand with `kinhin toolchains prune [--dry-run]`. `kinhin doctor` reports the cache size and each project's
share state.

---

Source: https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/requeue-skip.md

# Requeue and skip queued jobs

The Fleet tab now lets you re-queue or drop the fleet's queued jobs, per forge, from
the **Requeue / skip queued** row (one button per attached forge).

## Where it appears

Every attached forge gets a row in the "Requeue / skip queued" section with a
**Requeue** and **Skip** button:

```
Requeue / skip queued
  github
    [Requeue] [Skip]
  gitea
    [Requeue] [Skip]
```

The per-forge choice of scope is shown with a small menu on each row:

- **Org scope** (no slash in the forge's scope): the faucet is fleet-wide, so
  the button re-queues/skips the whole fleet's queue across *every* attached forge.
- **Repo scope** (a slash like `acme/widgets`): the button targets only that one
  forge.

A **Start/Stop is in flight** disables all four buttons — the same state backstop
as the Stop/Pause row.

## What they do

`FleetController.requeueQueuedJobs(for:)` and `FleetController.skipQueuedJobs(for:)`
are the throwing app-facing actions. Both:

1. Guard against a command already running (`pendingFleetAction`).
2. Dispatch through whichever backend is live — the in-process engine or the
   daemon — via `FleetBackend`.
3. Run the engine operation, then **refresh the status** so the UI shows the
   re-queued/dropped work coming back or draining.

The engine operation itself lives on each queue-capable forge. GitHub (the only
queue-capable forge today) is implemented through the GitHub client's
`cancelWorkflowRun(ids:)` / `skipWorkflowRun(ids:)`. `EngineError.forgeNotFound`
is raised when the requested forge has no queue implementation.

The in-VM work is unchanged — these operations only touch the forge's queue of
queued jobs, never a running job or instance.

## Adding a queue-capable forge

A forge supports requeue/skip by conforming to the `ForgeWithQueuedJobs` protocol
in `KinhinKit/Forges/Forge.swift`:

```swift
public protocol ForgeWithQueuedJobs: Forge {
    func userRequeueQueuedJobs() async throws
    func userSkipQueuedJobs() async throws
}
```

The engine dispatches `(requeue|skip)QueuedJobs(for:)` on the engine itself to
the concrete forge type; no fleet-controller change is needed. The requirements
are:

- `userRequeueQueuedJobs()` cancels the queued jobs matching the fleet's labels
  and re-queues them downstream.
- `userSkipQueuedJobs()` drops those jobs as skipped.

Only the client of that forge needs to answer `cancelWorkflowRun(ids:)` /
`skipWorkflowRun(ids:)` (which accepts a run id — work with fine-grained
granularity, not the job's numeric id) and return whether each was dropped.

## UI and failure handling

- A denied or failed requeue/skip surfaces an alert titled
  *"Couldn't requeue the queued jobs"* / *"Couldn't skip the queued jobs"* via
  `AlertKit`, with the pending flag cleared.
- A failed command is followed by a fresh status poll so the tab shows the state
  the backend actually settled into.
- The buttons disable while a start/stop is in flight, and a second click while
  busy is a no-op.

## Managing the fleet from the CLI

The `kinhin` headless CLI drives the fleet's lifecycle and its queued-job queue.
Queue operations dispatch through the live backend (daemon or, in the app, the
in-process engine) the same way the Fleet tab does.

| Command | What it does |
| ------- | ------------ |
| `kinhin start` | Starts the fleet in the current terminal (Ctrl-C to stop). Runs the engine in-process and opens no control socket, so `status`, `stop`, `pause` and `watch` cannot see it (`status` reports `daemonRunning: false`); use `kinhin daemon` when you need them. |
| `kinhin stop` | Stops the fleet through the daemon (it prints that no daemon is running otherwise; a fleet started with `kinhin start` stops with Ctrl-C). It is not a drain: it deletes every active VM, ending any job running on one. `kinhin pause` first lets running jobs finish. |
| `kinhin pause` / `kinhin resume` | Hold the fleet / let it scale again. Requires a running daemon. |
| `kinhin status [--json]` | Show fleet status (queue depth, VMs, jobs). Attach to the daemon if running. |
| `kinhin watch` | Live status view, refreshes every 2s. |
| `kinhin daemon` | Run the headless daemon in the current terminal. |
| `kinhin requeue <forge> [--yes]` | Cancel the fleet's queued jobs on a forge and re-queue them. Requires the daemon; prints the dry-run intent unless `--yes` confirms. |
| `kinhin skip <forge> [--yes]` | Mark the fleet's queued jobs on a forge as skipped. Requires the daemon; prints the dry-run intent unless `--yes` confirms. |
| `kinhin logs [-n N]` / `kinhin cleanup` | Logs and disk-reclamation commands. |

### Requeue and skip

`kinhin requeue <forge>` and `kinhin skip <forge>` talk to the daemon over the
same `requeue_queued_jobs` / `skip_queued_jobs` RPC methods the app uses; the CLI
has no in-process backend of its own. Before dispatching, each command:

1. Parses `<forge>` as a `ForgeID` (unknown values list the forges already in
   config or the known forges and suggest adding the forge first).
2. Prints the dry-run intent (`would requeue …` / `would skip …`) unless
   `--yes` is given, so headless scripts can preview without side effects.
3. Fails with `no daemon running; requeue/skip works while a daemon is active`
   when the daemon is absent.

Pending-state backstop, the in-app `AlertKit` failure alert, and the
refresh-after-command path live in the app's `FleetController` and its App Intent
bridge, so the Fleet tab buttons and status-bar menu keep their UX. The CLI path
is the unattended / remote complement: run the daemon on the Mac, then
`kinhin requeue github --yes` or `kinhin skip github --yes` from another terminal
or script.

## Tests

`Tests/KinhinAppTests/FleetRequeueSkipTests.swift` covers pending state, backend
dispatch, refresh after success, failure surfacing, and the no-backend throw.

## Verification and CI

The fleet requeue/skip path is covered by two suites: `Tests/KinhinAppTests/FleetRequeueSkipTests`
(controller actions, pending state, refresh, AlertKit failure surfacing, no-backend throw) and
`Tests/KinhinAppTests/FleetDetailModelTests` (filter behavior, breakdown rendering, drill-down).
Both use the `FakeFleetServing` test double, which records `requeueQueuedJobs(for:)` and
`skipQueuedJobs(for:)` calls so CI can assert pending-state and backend dispatch precisely.

The CI build and test sequence is:

```bash
swift build
swift test
swift format lint --strict -r Sources Tests
bash scripts/docs-refs.sh check
```

`swift test` runs the full `KinhinAppTests`, `KinhinKitTests`, and `KinhinCLITests` trees
including the new `FleetRequeueSkipTests` and `FleetDetailModelTests`. The CI gate is green
when the build compiles, the suites pass, and the strict formatter reports no new deviations.

## See also

- [How scaling works](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/scaling.md) — the queue/running breakdown this row feeds.

Source: https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/healing.md

# The healing agent

kinhin watches its own fleet for problems and fixes the ones it safely can. A warm VM that was deleted behind its
back, a toolchain cache filling the disk, an account that dropped off for a minute: these are fixed on their own.
Anything destructive or slow (pruning images, reinstalling a runtime) waits for you to approve it. Anything only you
can do (a new token, an image bake) is shown with the exact command.

An advisor can also be asked about problems no rule covers: the on-device Apple Intelligence model on a Mac with it (macOS
26 or later), or your own models on [Ollama](#the-ollama-advisor). It may only pick from the fixes kinhin allows for that
problem, and it can never make a fix run that would otherwise wait for you. The on-device model sends nothing off your
Mac; an Ollama host that is not this Mac receives the redacted problem and log lines.

[← Back to README](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/index.md) · [How scaling works](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/scaling.md) · [Troubleshooting](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/troubleshooting.md)

## What it does on its own, and what it asks first

Every fix has a fixed tier: **automatic** (runs on its own), **approval** (waits for you) or **yours** (only you can do
it; kinhin says how). The rules, the advisor and the config can lower what runs on its own, never raise it.

| Problem | Fix | Tier |
| ------- | --- | ---- |
| A warm VM (or any instance nothing is driving) was stopped or deleted outside kinhin | Remove its record and leftovers; a replacement starts if work is waiting (the engine's own sweep, every 2 minutes, with healing on or off; journaled when healing is on) | Automatic |
| Spawns are held on disk pressure | Prune the toolchain cache by its `toolchain_cache:` policy, and surplus per-project images (only when `auto_prune` is on) | Automatic |
| ...and the disk is still full after that (or `auto_prune` is off) | Prune unused images, as `kinhin image prune --yes` does | Approval |
| An account dropped off (timeout, unreachable server) for a minute | Re-attach it now instead of waiting out its backoff | Automatic |
| An account was refused (401/403, bad token) | `kinhin auth set --account NAME` | Yours |
| A token is missing or the Keychain cannot be read | `kinhin auth set` | Yours |
| The Apple container system is not running | `container system start` | Automatic |
| A runtime is missing (its setup check fails, or its runners keep failing) | Install it, as `kinhin setup repair <runtime>` does | Approval |
| Tart is killed on launch or broken | Reinstall, or roll back to the notarized build | Approval |
| An image is not prepared | `kinhin image prepare` | Yours |
| Another runtime or image setup check fails | The fix `kinhin setup status` lists | Yours |
| A teardown has kept failing for 10 minutes | Remove the instance with its runtime, then `kinhin cleanup --vms` | Yours |
| A queue unreadable for 2 minutes, a reconcile pass failing for 2 minutes, runners that keep failing on a healthy runtime | No rule: the advisor is asked if one is available, otherwise it is shown to you | Depends on the pick |

Tart setup checks (tart itself, its rollback, the base image) only count when the fleet can run Tart VMs: Tart is the
default runtime, a route names it, `images:` has entries, or `warm_pool` is set. A Docker-only fleet is never told to
install tart.

The engine's own retries keep running underneath: spawn backoff, orphan sweeps, teardown retries and forge re-attach
backoff all work with healing off. The agent adds what they do not cover, and gives every problem one place to look.

## How it decides

The agent runs in its own loop beside the scaling loop, every 30 seconds, so a slow fix or a slow model never delays
scaling. On each pass it collects the current problems from the status alerts, the instance records, the spawn backoff
and the setup checks, one entry per problem. The setup checklist runs once when the fleet starts, then again (at most
every 5 minutes) only while it reports a problem or runners keep failing to start: a healthy fleet does not re-run it.

- **It waits before acting.** An account must stay detached for a minute, a queue read or a reconcile pass must keep
  failing for 2 minutes, and a teardown for 10 minutes; a one-off failure heals by itself.
- **It tries each fix a few times.** A fix is tried at most `max_attempts` times for one problem, at least 2 minutes
  apart. A fix that ran and succeeded but left the problem in place counts as spent, and the next fix in the list is
  tried.
- **Then it escalates once.** When no fix is left (or the problem has no rule), the advisor is asked once, if one is
  available and there is anything it may pick. Otherwise the problem is shown to you. If the advisor's fix runs and the
  problem is still there after the cooldown, that is shown to you too, once.
- **It forgets what went away.** A problem that goes away closes its open entries ("went away"), and the next time it
  happens kinhin starts over with a fresh budget.

A fix that waits for approval, or a problem shown to you, stays open until you act, dismiss it, or the problem goes
away. Nothing new is tried for that problem in the meantime.

## `kinhin heal`

```bash
kinhin heal                   # policy, fixes waiting for approval, problems that need you, recent history
kinhin heal --json            # the same as a document
kinhin heal --quiet           # nothing printed; the exit code is the answer
kinhin heal approve h-8d04e7c2
kinhin heal dismiss h-8d04e7c2
```

A fleet that pruned its cache on its own and now waits to prune images:

```text
$ kinhin heal
healing: safe fixes run on their own; rules only

waiting for approval (kinhin heal approve ID):
  h-8d04e7c2  prune unused images needs approval: disk pressure: 18 GB free, a new docker instance needs 8 GB + 20 GB reserve — holding spawns

recent:
  h-5e1a90d3  succeeded 3m ago  freed 2048 MB from 37 cache entr(ies)
  h-3f9c21ab  succeeded 12m ago  removed kinhin-1760432400-a1b2; a replacement starts if work is waiting
```

Problems only you can fix are listed under `needs you (kinhin heal dismiss ID once handled):`. The history shows the
last 10 closed entries. With `healing.enabled: false` the command only says that healing is off.

`approve` starts the fix in the background and returns at once (an install can take minutes); run `kinhin heal` again
to see how it ended. `dismiss` closes a pending or shown entry and leaves that problem alone until it goes away.

`kinhin heal` talks to the daemon. With no daemon it says so and prints the history the last one left (up to 10
entries); entries that were still open read as `expired`, since nobody can act on them now. A problem that persists is
raised again when the fleet starts.

| Command | Exit code |
| ------- | --------- |
| `kinhin heal` | 0 when nothing waits on you; 1 when a fix waits for approval, a problem needs you, or no daemon runs; 4 when the daemon cannot answer (one that predates healing: restart it) |
| `kinhin heal approve ID`, `kinhin heal dismiss ID` | 0 done; 1 no daemon; 2 no ID, or an ID that is not in the journal; 4 an entry that is not waiting on you (already approved, ran or closed) |

### The JSON document

Printed with sorted keys and ISO 8601 dates. The MCP `heal_status` tool returns the same document.

| Field | Meaning |
| ----- | ------- |
| `daemon` | False when no daemon answered; `pending` and `surfaced` are then empty and `events` is the stored history |
| `enabled`, `automatic` | `healing.enabled`, and whether `healing.auto` is `safe` |
| `advisor` | The advisor consulted (`apple-intelligence`, or `ollama:<model>`); absent when there is none |
| `pending` | Fixes waiting for approval, newest first |
| `surfaced` | Problems only you can fix, newest first |
| `events` | The whole journal, newest first (`kinhin status` carries only the open entries and the 10 newest closed ones) |
| `message` | Only when no daemon answered: why |

Each entry has an `id`, the `signal` (its `kind`, `subject` and `detail`, plus `evidence` or `setupAction` when the
engine probed), the `remediation` (`kind` and `subject`; absent when nothing fits and the problem is only shown), the
`source` (`playbook` or `advisor`), the `outcome`, a token-free `detail`, the advisor's `explanation` when it picked
the fix, and `createdAt` / `updatedAt`. Outcomes: `pending`, `running`, `succeeded`, `failed`, `surfaced`,
`dismissed`, `resolved` (the problem went away first) and `expired` (left open when the fleet stopped).

```json
{
  "automatic" : true,
  "daemon" : true,
  "enabled" : true,
  "events" : [
    {
      "createdAt" : "2026-10-14T09:20:00Z",
      "detail" : "prune unused images needs approval: disk pressure: 18 GB free, a new docker instance needs 8 GB + 20 GB reserve — holding spawns",
      "id" : "h-8d04e7c2",
      "outcome" : "pending",
      "remediation" : {
        "kind" : "prune_images"
      },
      "signal" : {
        "detail" : "disk pressure: 18 GB free, a new docker instance needs 8 GB + 20 GB reserve — holding spawns",
        "kind" : "disk_pressure"
      },
      "source" : "playbook",
      "updatedAt" : "2026-10-14T09:20:00Z"
    }
  ],
  "pending" : [
    {
      "createdAt" : "2026-10-14T09:20:00Z",
      "detail" : "prune unused images needs approval: disk pressure: 18 GB free, a new docker instance needs 8 GB + 20 GB reserve — holding spawns",
      "id" : "h-8d04e7c2",
      "outcome" : "pending",
      "remediation" : {
        "kind" : "prune_images"
      },
      "signal" : {
        "detail" : "disk pressure: 18 GB free, a new docker instance needs 8 GB + 20 GB reserve — holding spawns",
        "kind" : "disk_pressure"
      },
      "source" : "playbook",
      "updatedAt" : "2026-10-14T09:20:00Z"
    }
  ],
  "surfaced" : [

  ]
}
```

### Elsewhere

- A pending fix raises a `healing` alert in `kinhin status` ("1 fix(es) need approval — run `kinhin heal`"), which
  the app turns into a "kinhin needs attention" notification.
- The app posts "kinhin fixed a problem" each time a fix succeeds.
- The app's Diagnostics sheet has a Healing card: the policy, the fixes waiting for approval (Approve, Dismiss), the
  problems that need you (Dismiss), what is running and the last 10 closed entries. When the app runs the fleet in its
  own process instead of the daemon, this card is where healing shows.
- The MCP server's `heal_status` tool is read-only: approving a fix stays with a person.

## Fixes and what they run

Every fix goes through a code path kinhin already uses elsewhere; nothing runs a command a person or a model wrote. The
kind is what `remediation.kind` says in the journal.

| Kind | Tier | What runs |
| ---- | ---- | --------- |
| `recycle_instance` | Automatic | The engine's normal removal of one instance (record and leftovers), then the scaler is woken |
| `retry_forge_attach` | Automatic | Every detached account is re-attached now, skipping its backoff; fails if the account stays detached |
| `prune_toolchain_cache` | Automatic | The cache prune `kinhin toolchains prune` runs, with your `toolchain_cache:` policy, then derived per-project images beyond `max_project_images` or older than `max_age_days` (images in use stay) |
| `start_container_system` | Automatic | `container system start` |
| `prune_images` | Approval | The plan `kinhin image prune --yes` runs: stale records and unused local images across Tart, Apple container and Docker; images the fleet uses stay |
| `repair_runtime` | Approval | The installer `kinhin setup repair <runtime>` runs (for host, the runner agents); nothing when it is already installed |
| `repair_tart` | Approval | The first repair the tart health check lists (reinstall, or roll back to the notarized build), each command allowed 30 minutes |
| `replace_token` | Yours | Shown: `kinhin auth set --account NAME` |
| `prepare_image` | Yours | Shown: `kinhin image prepare` |
| `inspect_instance` | Yours | Shown: delete the instance with its runtime (`tart delete`, `docker rm -f` or `container delete`), then `kinhin cleanup --vms` |
| `review_setup` | Yours | Shown: run `kinhin setup status` and use the fix it lists |

## Config

```yaml
healing:
  enabled: true      # false = only the engine's own retries; nothing new is fixed or journaled
  auto: safe         # safe = automatic-tier fixes run on their own; none = every fix waits for approval
  ai: auto           # auto = Apple Intelligence advises on problems no rule covers; off = rules only; ollama = see below
  max_attempts: 3    # tries of one fix for one problem before it escalates (1-10)
  ollama:            # only with ai: ollama
    model: my-llm                  # the LLM: any model you pulled, or built with `ollama create`
    fast_model: clef-flash         # optional System 1 decision model, asked first
    host: http://127.0.0.1:11434   # the default; a host that is not this Mac must be https
```

Every key is optional; the values above are the defaults, except `ollama`, which `ai: ollama` requires with a `model`.
Any other value is a config error (exit 3) that names the key. Changing them rebuilds the engine (instances are kept,
open entries expire and are raised again if the problem persists).

## The on-device advisor

The advisor is Apple Intelligence through Apple's Foundation Models framework, running in the process that runs the
fleet. For a problem it is asked about, it gets:

- the problem as kinhin sees it (no tokens: every message is redacted first),
- the fixes kinhin allows for that problem's subject (a VM, an account, a runtime, the disk), minus the ones already
  spent, and
- up to 40 recent log lines about it (warnings and errors when the problem has no subject), trimmed to fit the model's
  window.

It answers in one structured generation: one of those fixes or none (the answer's schema only allows those ids),
whether it is sure, and one sentence of reasoning that the journal shows next to the entry. kinhin checks the answer again: a fix outside the list is ignored and logged, an
approval-tier fix still waits for you, and a pick the model is not sure about is only shown ("suggests …, but is not
sure"). Tokens and setup problems are never offered to the model. The answer has 20 seconds; if the model is slow or
unavailable, the problem is shown to you as if there were no advisor. Whether
the model is ready is checked again every 10 minutes.

The explanation is for reading only and can be wrong about the cause. It never drives an action.

**Requirements:** macOS 26 or later on Apple Silicon with Apple Intelligence turned on. Every kinhin build includes
the advisor; on macOS 15, or with Apple Intelligence off or its model still downloading, kinhin runs the rules only and
`kinhin heal` says "rules only".

## The Ollama advisor

With `ai: ollama`, the advisor is a model on an [Ollama](https://ollama.com) server, and you choose the models. There
are two tiers, and the answer comes from the first one that is confident:

1. **System 1 (`fast_model`, optional):** a decision model such as `clef-flash` or `nimble`, on Ollama's
   `/v1/systemone` endpoint. It does not write text: it gives each allowed fix a probability. A fix at 80% or more is a
   confident answer, and System 1's answer is final.
2. **The LLM (`model`):** any Ollama chat model, asked through `/api/chat` with a schema that allows only the allowed
   fixes or `none`. It is asked when System 1 is not confident, picks nothing, or is not configured.

If the LLM does not answer, System 1's answer stands, and a doubtful answer is only shown, as with the on-device model.
The LLM's "confident" is its own judgment, so a confident LLM pick is queued for approval (`kinhin heal approve ID`) rather
than run, even when the fix is automatic. A confident System 1 pick runs on its own, as its probability is measured.
A System 1 answer's journal entry names its model (`System 1 (clef-flash) chose …`); `kinhin heal` names the LLM as the
advisor. Without `fast_model`, the LLM alone advises.

```bash
ollama serve                 # if it is not already running
ollama pull clef-flash       # the System 1 model (optional); needs Ollama 0.35.1 or later
ollama pull <your-llm>       # or: ollama create my-llm -f Modelfile
```

`nimble-v3` needs Ollama 0.40.4 or later. It is licensed for noncommercial use only (CC BY-NC 4.0), so check its license
before you use it. `clef-flash` is Apache 2.0. kinhin checks that the server is up, that the model is pulled, and that
the version is new enough, every 10 minutes. A check that fails is shown as "rules only" with the reason in the log.

**What is sent:** the same redacted problem, allowed fixes and log lines as the on-device advisor (see above). With
`host` on this Mac (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `::1`), nothing leaves the machine. With any other host, those redacted
lines are sent to that host, so kinhin requires `https` for it. Point `host` only at a server you trust with your
fleet's logs.

## What healing does not do

- It never stores, reads or replaces a token, and never edits your config.
- It never runs a free-form command. The advisor can only pick from the list above; it cannot add to it.
- It does not start long jobs on its own: image bakes and installs wait for you.
- It does not fix failed CI jobs in your repositories, only the fleet that runs them.
- It does not act on setup checks outside runtimes and images (config, Command Line Tools, architecture): those stop a
  fleet before there is anything to heal.
- It does not touch instances kinhin has no record of; the orphan sweep handles those.
- It does not coordinate between Macs. Each Mac heals its own fleet.

## Where things live

| What | Where |
| ---- | ----- |
| The journal (last 100 entries, owner-only) | `~/Library/Application Support/Kinhin/state/healing.json` |
| Log lines | `kinhin logs`, component `healing` |
| The rules | `Sources/KinhinKit/Fleet/Healing/HealingPlaybook.swift` |
| The design | [plans/healing-agent.md](https://github.com/RabinApps/kinhin/blob/v0.0.1-beta-4/docs/plans/healing-agent.md) |

---

Source: https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/telemetry.md

# Telemetry (OpenTelemetry)

kinhin can export metrics, traces and logs about the fleet and the jobs it runs over [OTLP](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otlp/),
and serve the metrics on a local Prometheus endpoint. It is **off by default**: until you turn it on, kinhin starts no exporter, opens no
port and sends nothing anywhere.

The OpenTelemetry Swift SDK is pinned to an exact release. Upstream marks traces stable and metrics and logs as still in development, so
expect the odd rough edge in those two signals, and treat this feature as beta.

## Turn it on

```yaml
telemetry:
  enabled: true
  endpoint: http://localhost:4318   # your collector (Grafana Alloy, the OpenTelemetry Collector, …)
```

That exports all three signals over OTLP/HTTP every 60 seconds. After you edit the file, run `kinhin config reload`. The running daemon applies the change in place: no
engine restart, no duplicate exporters, and a Prometheus port from the old settings is released first.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `false` | Master switch. Nothing below does anything while it is false (except `log_format`). |
| `endpoint` | `http://localhost:4318` (`:4317` for gRPC) | Collector base URL, `http` or `https`. For HTTP/protobuf kinhin appends `/v1/metrics`, `/v1/traces` and `/v1/logs`. |
| `protocol` | `http/protobuf` | `http/protobuf` or `grpc`. |
| `export_interval_seconds` | `60` | Seconds between metric pushes and between span and log batches (1–3600). `export_interval` is accepted as an alias. |
| `signals` | all three | Any subset of `metrics`, `traces`, `logs`. |
| `resource_attributes` | none | Extra resource attributes. `service.name`, `service.version` and `telemetry.sdk.*` belong to kinhin and are rejected here. |
| `prometheus_listen` | off | `host:port`, or a bare port, which binds `127.0.0.1`. Serves `GET /metrics`. Needs `metrics` in `signals`. |
| `log_format` | `text` | `json` writes one JSON object per line to `kinhin.log` and stderr. Independent of `enabled`. |
| `job_attributes` | none | `[repository, workflow]` adds those dimensions to the job counters and histograms. See [Cardinality](#cardinality-and-privacy). |
| `sampling_ratio` | `1` | Share of job traces recorded and exported, from `0` to `1`. See [Sampling, severity, credentials and TLS](#sampling-severity-credentials-and-tls). |
| `log_level` | `info` | `debug`, `info`, `warn` or `error`: the lowest severity sent over OTLP. Independent of the local log. |
| `headers_keychain` | none | Name of a Keychain item holding a collector token, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. |
| `ca_file` | system roots | Absolute path (or `~/…`) of a PEM CA bundle that signs the collector's `https` certificate. Checked when the config loads. |
| `persist` | `false` | `true` queues spans and log records on disk, so they survive collector downtime and daemon restarts. |

Credentials are never read from `config.yaml`. Put collector headers in `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` in the environment of the process that
runs the engine (for the daemon, its LaunchAgent environment). kinhin never logs them, and registers their values with the log redactor.

## Environment variables

Standard `OTEL_*` variables take precedence over the matching config key. The SDK does not apply them uniformly across signals, so kinhin
reads these itself and honours exactly this list:

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true` | Telemetry stays off whatever the config says. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | Overrides `endpoint`. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_{TRACES,METRICS,LOGS}_ENDPOINT` | A full per-signal URL, used as given (no path appended). |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL` | `http/protobuf` or `grpc`. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` | `key=value,key2=value2` request headers (credentials). |
| `OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL` | Milliseconds (1000–3600000). |
| `OTEL_{METRICS,TRACES,LOGS}_EXPORTER=none` | Removes that signal. |
| `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES` | `key=value,…`, merged over `resource_attributes`. |

The environment never turns telemetry **on**; only `telemetry.enabled: true` does. A value kinhin cannot use is ignored and logged as a warning.
`OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` is not honoured: the service is always `kinhin`, so dashboards keyed on it keep working.

### Resource attributes

Precedence, lowest to highest: host defaults (`host.name`, `host.arch`, `os.type`, `os.version`, `service.instance.id`), then
`resource_attributes`, then `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES`, then kinhin's own identity (`service.name=kinhin`, `service.version`, and the SDK's
`telemetry.sdk.*`), which nothing can override.

## Sampling, severity, credentials and TLS

**Sampling.** `sampling_ratio: 0.1` records one job trace in ten. The decision is made once per job at its root span, from the trace ID, so
a kept trace is complete and a dropped one has no spans at all (its log lines carry no trace ID either). Metrics are never sampled. The
environment overrides it: `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` (`always_on`, `always_off`, `traceidratio`, `parentbased_traceidratio`) with
`OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG` (the ratio, 0 to 1). `kinhin telemetry status` shows the ratio when it is below 1.

**Log severity.** `log_level` filters only what is forwarded to the OTLP log pipeline. It is independent of the local log: the file, stderr
and the app's log view follow `Log.minLevel` (info), whatever `log_level` says, and a `debug` here sends debug records to the collector even
though the local file does not keep them.

**Collector token from the Keychain.** `headers_keychain: grafana-cloud` reads the item stored for that name and sends it as
`Authorization: Bearer <token>`, unless `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` already sets `authorization`, which wins. The token is never in
`config.yaml`, is masked in logs, and is not shown by `status`. If the item is missing or the Keychain refuses, telemetry still starts
without the header and logs one warning naming the account. Store the token once (it is read by the daemon, so allow it when macOS asks):

```sh
security add-generic-password -U -s com.kinhin.runner -a telemetry:grafana-cloud -w
```

`-w` with no value prompts for it, so it stays out of your shell history. A config reload re-reads the item, so rotating the token restarts
the exporters.

**TLS.** `ca_file` (or `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_CERTIFICATE`, which wins) makes kinhin trust only that CA bundle for the collector, over OTLP/HTTP
and gRPC, instead of the system roots. The file must exist and hold at least one PEM certificate, or the config does not load (a bad
environment value stops telemetry from starting instead). It has no effect on an `http` endpoint, and kinhin warns. Client certificates
(mTLS) are not supported.

**Persistence.** `persist: true` writes spans and log records to `~/Library/Application Support/Kinhin/telemetry-queue/` (owner-only) before
sending and deletes them once the collector accepts them, so an outage or a daemon restart does not lose them. The queue is capped at 32 MB
per signal (the oldest files go first) and anything older than 12 hours is dropped unsent. Metrics are not queued: they are cumulative, and
the next successful push carries the totals. Keep it off unless you need it; queued records hold job and repository names on disk.

## Metrics

Names use dots; Prometheus shows them with underscores (`cicd_worker_count`). Durations are in seconds, sizes in bytes, utilisation is a ratio.
Names and attributes follow the [OpenTelemetry CI/CD semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/cicd/) where one
exists (`cicd.worker.*`, `cicd.pipeline.*`, `cicd.system.*`, `error.type`) and are `kinhin.`-prefixed otherwise.

| Metric | Kind | Attributes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cicd.worker.count` | gauge | `kinhin.pool`, `kinhin.image`, `kinhin.runner.labels` (sorted), `cicd.worker.state` (the lifecycle phase) |
| `kinhin.queue.depth` | gauge | `kinhin.account` |
| `kinhin.queue.pool.depth` | gauge | `kinhin.pool` |
| `kinhin.queue.age` | gauge | none. The oldest queued job; only while the forge reports when jobs were queued |
| `kinhin.fleet.desired`, `.active`, `.paused`, `.running` | gauge | none |
| `kinhin.pool.capacity` | gauge | `kinhin.pool` |
| `kinhin.warm_pool.size` | gauge | `kinhin.pool`, `kinhin.image` |
| `kinhin.warm_pool.claims`, `.evictions` | counter | `kinhin.pool`, `kinhin.image`, `kinhin.runner.labels`, `kinhin.forge` |
| `kinhin.jobs.picked_up` | counter | `kinhin.pool`, `kinhin.image`, `kinhin.runner.labels`, `kinhin.forge` |
| `kinhin.jobs.completed` | counter | the same, plus `cicd.pipeline.result` (+ `job_attributes`) |
| `cicd.pipeline.run.active` | gauge | none |
| `cicd.pipeline.run.duration` | histogram | `kinhin.pool`, `kinhin.image`, `kinhin.runner.labels`, `kinhin.forge`, `cicd.pipeline.result` (+ `job_attributes`) |
| `kinhin.job.queue_wait.duration` | histogram | `kinhin.pool`, `kinhin.image`, `kinhin.runner.labels`, `kinhin.forge` (+ `job_attributes`). Only with provider timestamps |
| `kinhin.runner.provision.duration` | histogram | the pool attributes plus `kinhin.runner.phase` (`clone`, `boot`, `register`) |
| `kinhin.runner.teardown.duration` | histogram | `kinhin.pool`, `kinhin.image`, `kinhin.runner.labels`, `kinhin.forge` |
| `kinhin.runner.cpu.utilization`, `.memory.usage`, `.memory.limit` | gauge | `kinhin.pool`, `kinhin.image`, `kinhin.runner.labels`. Aggregated over runners |
| `kinhin.runner.disk.usage` | gauge | `kinhin.pool`, `kinhin.image`, `kinhin.runner.labels`. Host disk the runner VMs occupy, summed over runners (tart reports whole GB); tart only |
| `kinhin.image.bake.duration` | histogram | `kinhin.image`, `kinhin.result` (`success`, `failure`). Derived per-project image bakes run by the daemon |
| `kinhin.image.bakes` | counter | the same |
| `kinhin.cache.size` | gauge | `kinhin.cache` (`toolchain`). Sampled at the daily cache sweep, so it can be up to a day old; absent until the first sweep |
| `kinhin.cache.prunes` | counter | `kinhin.result` (`success`, `failure`: some entries could not be deleted). One per daily sweep that pruned |
| `kinhin.host.cpu.utilization`, `.memory.usage`, `.memory.limit`, `.disk.free` | gauge | none |
| `process.cpu.utilization`, `process.memory.usage` | gauge | none (the daemon process) |
| `kinhin.forge.api.requests` | counter | `kinhin.forge`, `http.response.status_class` (`2xx`…`5xx`, `error`) |
| `kinhin.forge.rate_limit.remaining`, `.limit` | gauge | `kinhin.forge`, `kinhin.account` |
| `kinhin.healing.actions` | counter | `kinhin.healing.result` (`succeeded`, `failed`) |
| `kinhin.healing.awaiting_approval` | gauge | none |
| `kinhin.build.info` | gauge | `service.version` (value 1) |
