| `kinhin.daemon.uptime` | gauge | none (seconds since the engine started) |
| `kinhin.reconcile.duration` | histogram | none (one control-loop pass) |
| `kinhin.reconcile.last_success` | gauge | none (Unix time of the last completed pass; alert on `time()` minus it) |
| `kinhin.reconcile.errors` | counter | none |
| `kinhin.spawn.failures` | counter | `kinhin.pool` |
| `kinhin.spawn.held` | gauge | `kinhin.pool`, `kinhin.spawn.hold_reason` (`backoff`, `disk_pressure`); absent when nothing is held |
| `kinhin.telemetry.export.failures` | counter | none |
| `cicd.system.errors` | counter | `error.type`, `cicd.system.component` (`lifecycle`, `forge`) |

`error.type` is one of `clone_failed`, `boot_timeout`, `ssh_unreachable`, `registration_failed`, `runner_not_registered`, `instance_lost`,
`forge_api`, `rate_limited`, `teardown_failed`, `unknown`. Never the error text.

**The job result is the forge's, or `unknown`.** When a job ends kinhin asks the forge, once, what happened. GitHub, GitLab,
Buildkite, Gitea, Forgejo and Azure DevOps answer with the job's verdict and its own start and end times (GitHub also with its steps): `cicd.pipeline.result` is then
`success`, `failure`, `cancellation`, `timeout` or `skip`, the run duration uses the forge's times, and on GitHub the trace gets one span per
step. Bitbucket (its API does not say which runner took a step, so a step cannot be tied to a VM), a job the forge has not yet marked finished after a few short retries, and a job kinhin never saw running read
`unknown`. kinhin never guesses a verdict. The read happens while the instance is torn down, so it adds no delay. To learn which job a runner
took, kinhin asks the forge for the running jobs as soon as the runner turns busy; a job that finishes in about a second can still outrun
that and read `unknown`. `cicd.system.errors` counts kinhin's own failures, not failing workflows.

**Unavailable is not zero.** When a runtime or forge cannot supply a value, that series is absent. Today that means: per-runner disk use on
runtimes other than tart, and for a VM where tart reports no on-disk size, `kinhin.cache.size` before the first daily sweep or when
there is no cache directory, `kinhin.queue.age` and the queue-wait histogram on forges that do not report queue timestamps (GitHub does, through
the job's `created_at`), and CPU on the first sample after a start. SSH-ready is not timed apart from boot because the runtimes do not
separate them: `boot` covers both.

### Cardinality and privacy

VM names, job and run IDs and trace and span IDs are **never** metric attributes: they appear only on spans and log records. Metric attributes
come from small closed sets (pool, image, forge, account, phase, result, error type, component) and the sorted runner labels from your config.
Per-repository and per-workflow dimensions are off by default: in an org-scoped fleet they are unbounded, and each combination is a series
in Prometheus or Mimir. `job_attributes: [repository, workflow]` adds them (as `vcs.repository.name` and `cicd.pipeline.name`) to
`kinhin.jobs.completed`, `cicd.pipeline.run.duration` and the queue-wait histogram only, and only where the forge supplied the value. Turn them
on for a fleet with a known, small set of repositories; otherwise use traces, which carry them for free. Runner CPU and memory are aggregated per pool and image, never one series per VM.

Logs pass through the same redaction as the local log before export; tokens and registration secrets cannot reach a collector or the JSON log.
Spans and logs do carry repository, workflow and job names and VM names, so only point `endpoint` at a collector you trust with them.

## Traces

One trace per instance, from spawn to teardown. The root span `kinhin.job` carries `kinhin.vm.id`, `kinhin.runner.name`, `kinhin.pool`, `kinhin.image`,
`kinhin.forge`, `kinhin.runner.labels`, the forge's `cicd.pipeline.result` and the final `kinhin.result`. Children, each only where there is a real measurement:

- `provision`, `boot_ready`, `registration`, `run`, `teardown`: timed by kinhin with the monotonic clock.
- `queue_wait`: from the forge's queue timestamp to its start timestamp, only when the forge supplied both.
- `step`: one per step the forge reports for the finished job, with the forge's own start and finish times (GitHub).

On GitHub Actions the root span also gets `cicd.pipeline.run.id`, `kinhin.run.attempt`, `kinhin.job.id`, `cicd.pipeline.name`,
`cicd.pipeline.task.name` and `vcs.repository.name` once the running job is seen. A job that starts and finishes between two polls is still
counted (the forge's completion signal is used), but it has no `run` span and no run duration, because nothing observed its start.

With `runners_per_vm` above 1 an instance runs several jobs: the root keeps the first job's identifiers, and each further job is a child
`job` span with its own, so nothing is overwritten. `kinhin.jobs.picked_up` still counts the instance once.

## Logs

With `logs` selected, every log line also becomes an OTLP log record with its severity, `kinhin.component`, the VM (`kinhin.vm.id`) and job
(`kinhin.job.name`, `kinhin.job.id`) when known, and the trace and span of the lifecycle it came from. `log_format: json` writes the same context locally:

```json
{"component":"kinhin-1717000000-a1b2c3d4","level":"info","message":"booted at 192.168.64.5","span_id":"…","trace_id":"…","ts":"2026-10-29T18:00:00.000Z","vm":"kinhin-1717000000-a1b2c3d4"}
```

`kinhin logs` and the app read the in-memory log, which is unaffected; only the file and stderr change shape.

## Prometheus

```yaml
telemetry:
  enabled: true
  signals: [metrics]
  prometheus_listen: 127.0.0.1:9464
```

`GET /metrics` serves the current metrics, collected at scrape time. Nothing else is served. `prometheus_listen` binds exactly the address you
write: a bare port or `127.0.0.1` stays on this Mac. **Binding `0.0.0.0` or a LAN address lets anyone who can reach that port read your fleet
metrics (pool names, labels, queue and capacity numbers) with no authentication.** kinhin logs a warning when you do; put a firewall or an
authenticating proxy in front of it. If the port cannot be bound, telemetry stays off and the error is logged.

## Reaching the collector

The daemon runs on the Mac and sends to `endpoint`, so `localhost` means the Mac. That is the right address for a collector on the same host.
Runner VMs and containers are separate machines to the network: a loopback address is **not** reachable from them, which matters only if you
forward telemetry from inside a job yourself.

## Checking it works

`kinhin telemetry status` (add `--json` for scripts) asks the daemon what the pipeline is doing: which signals, where each goes
(credentials and query strings removed), the bound Prometheus address, and the last export problem. The SDK never throws export
errors, so kinhin reports them itself: each distinct problem is logged at most once a minute as `export problem: …`, counted in
`kinhin.telemetry.export.failures`, and shown by `status`. It exits 1 when exports failed in the last five minutes, or when the config
enables telemetry and no daemon runs.

## Grafana Alloy, dashboards and alerts

A collector on the same Mac, forwarding to Grafana Cloud (Mimir for metrics, Loki for logs, Tempo for traces):

```alloy
otelcol.receiver.otlp "kinhin" {
  http { endpoint = "127.0.0.1:4318" }
  grpc { endpoint = "127.0.0.1:4317" }
  output {
    metrics = [otelcol.processor.batch.default.input]
    logs    = [otelcol.processor.batch.default.input]
    traces  = [otelcol.processor.batch.default.input]
  }
}

otelcol.processor.batch "default" {
  output {
    metrics = [otelcol.exporter.otlphttp.cloud.input]
    logs    = [otelcol.exporter.otlphttp.cloud.input]
    traces  = [otelcol.exporter.otlphttp.cloud.input]
  }
}

otelcol.auth.basic "cloud" {
  client_auth {
    username = sys.env("GRAFANA_CLOUD_INSTANCE_ID")
    password = sys.env("GRAFANA_CLOUD_TOKEN")
  }
}

otelcol.exporter.otlphttp "cloud" {
  client {
    endpoint = sys.env("GRAFANA_CLOUD_OTLP_ENDPOINT")
    auth     = otelcol.auth.basic.cloud.handler
  }
}
```

and in `config.yaml`:

```yaml
telemetry:
  enabled: true
  endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:4318
  resource_attributes: {deployment.environment: home}
```

To scrape metrics instead of pushing them, set `prometheus_listen: 127.0.0.1:9469` and add
`prometheus.scrape "kinhin" { targets = [{__address__ = "127.0.0.1:9469"}]  forward_to = [prometheus.remote_write.cloud.receiver]  job_name = "kinhin" }`.

Ready-made files live in the repository: [`docs/telemetry/kinhin-dashboard.json`](https://github.com/RabinApps/kinhin/blob/main/docs/telemetry/kinhin-dashboard.json)
(import it in Grafana and pick your Prometheus data source) and [`docs/telemetry/kinhin-alerts.yml`](https://github.com/RabinApps/kinhin/blob/main/docs/telemetry/kinhin-alerts.yml)
(queue stuck, fleet below desired, errors, forge rate limit, host disk, export failing, paused). Both use the names OTLP ingestion produces,
where counters end in `_total`; kinhin's own `/metrics` endpoint exposes counters without it. A test keeps every metric name in these files
in step with the catalog above.

## Who exports

The process that hosts the engine owns the exporters: the daemon, foreground `kinhin start`, or the menu bar app when it runs its own engine
because no daemon is up. An app attached to a daemon exports nothing; the daemon already does. The daemon and `kinhin start` flush on SIGTERM
and Ctrl-C; the app flushes when you quit it (waiting at most a few seconds, so a dead collector cannot hold up the quit), and only when it owns
the exporters.

The app has a **Telemetry** card under **Advanced → App**. It shows whether telemetry is on, the signals, where each goes (credentials and query
strings removed), the Prometheus address and the last export problem, read from the app's own pipeline or, when a daemon runs the fleet, from the
daemon (the same data as `kinhin telemetry status`). Its switch sets `telemetry.enabled` in `config.yaml`, and its address field sets
`telemetry.prometheus_listen`; both edit only that line, keep your comments and other keys, and apply in place without restarting the engine.
Everything else (endpoint, signals, headers) stays in the file and the environment.

## Limitations

- **Step-level trace propagation is not implemented.** kinhin does not pass `TRACEPARENT` or a collector address into workflow steps. It
  needs a per-job runner hook, proof that context cannot leak between reused runners, and an explicitly reachable collector. Daemon-side traces
  are complete without it.
- Job metrics (`picked_up`, `completed`, the run duration and the `run` span) need ephemeral or scale-set runners, the ones kinhin watches
  until their job ends. A classic persistent runner (`vm.ephemeral: false`) has lifecycle timings but no job counters.
- Job identifiers, queue times and a verdict come from GitHub Actions, GitLab, Buildkite, Gitea, Forgejo and Azure DevOps. Bitbucket gets
  the lifecycle spans and timings kinhin measures itself, and a result of `unknown`. On Gitea and Forgejo the job's end time is the task's
  last update, and the task is found in the newest 100 tasks; Azure DevOps has no separate `timeout` result. Step spans exist for GitHub only (the others have no step list).
- Metrics and logs in the upstream SDK are still in development; pin and test before relying on them.

---

Source: https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/workflow-testing.md

# Test a GitHub Actions workflow locally

`kinhin workflow test` runs a repository's GitHub Actions workflow scripts on your Mac before you push. It is a host-only convenience tool: it does not start the fleet, a VM, the daemon, or read kinhin's config or forge credentials. The Fleet tab also has **Test Workflow…**, which opens the same runner in a sheet after you choose a workflow file in Finder.

## CLI

Run from a checkout:

```sh
kinhin workflow test
kinhin workflow test --list
kinhin workflow test .github/workflows/ci.yml --job unit-tests
kinhin workflow test --json
```

With no file argument, kinhin uses the only `.yml` or `.yaml` file in `.github/workflows/`. If none exists, or more than one exists, it reports the problem and asks you to provide a file. `--list` shows each job's key, name, step count, and whether it has a matrix. `--job NAME` runs just that job, without its `needs:` jobs. `--json` suppresses progress output and emits the final report as JSON.

Exit codes follow the CLI convention: `0` all jobs succeeded, `1` a job failed or the result is only partial, `2` invalid command-line usage, `3` missing/invalid workflow YAML, and `130` cancellation with Ctrl-C.

### Partial results

Everything the runner cannot execute is skipped with a note: matrix jobs, `uses:` actions other than `actions/checkout`, and `if:` conditions outside the supported set. A run that skipped anything of that kind did not prove what a real runner would, so it is reported as `partial` (in the summary line and as `outcome` in `--json`, with the skipped items under `unsupportedSkips`) and exits `1`, even though every step that did run passed. `--lenient` accepts a partial result and exits `0`; a failed job still exits `1`. Deliberate skips (`if: false`, steps after an earlier failure) do not make a run partial.

Every run also prints a one-line note that steps run directly on this Mac, not isolated.

## Example

Save this as `.github/workflows/local-smoke.yml` in a checkout, then run `kinhin workflow test .github/workflows/local-smoke.yml`:

```yaml
name: Local smoke test

env:
  GREETING: Hello

jobs:
  smoke:
    name: Local smoke test
    steps:
      - name: Check the local runner environment
        run: |
          test -d "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE"
          echo "$GREETING, from $RUNNER_OS ($RUNNER_ARCH)"
```

The same complete workflow is checked in as [`Tests/Fixtures/workflow-local-smoke.yml`](https://github.com/RabinApps/kinhin/blob/v0.0.1-beta-4/Tests/Fixtures/workflow-local-smoke.yml); the runner test executes that fixture and checks the output below.

On an Apple Silicon Mac, the step prints `Hello, from macOS (arm64)` and the run ends with a succeeded summary. This example uses only local environment variables; it needs no checkout action, secrets, or network access. To inspect the job before running it, use `kinhin workflow test .github/workflows/local-smoke.yml --list`.

## What runs

Jobs run sequentially in dependency order. Each `run:` step is sent to a local `bash --noprofile --norc -e -o pipefail -s` (the flags GitHub uses; or a supported `sh`/`zsh`) process, rooted at the repository directory. Workflow, job, and step `env:` values and `defaults.run.working-directory`/`shell` are applied. `GITHUB_ENV` and `GITHUB_PATH` are temporary files; simple `KEY=VALUE` environment updates and added path lines affect later steps. Each step's output is captured and included in the final report, bounded to its most recent 200,000 characters.

The runner provides a small local environment: `CI`, `GITHUB_ACTIONS`, `GITHUB_WORKSPACE`, `RUNNER_OS=macOS`, and `RUNNER_ARCH=arm64`. It expands <code v-pre>${{ github.workspace }}</code>, <code v-pre>${{ runner.os }}</code>, <code v-pre>${{ runner.arch }}</code>, <code v-pre>${{ env.NAME }}</code>, and <code v-pre>${{ secrets.NAME }}</code>. Secrets are not available locally and expand to empty strings with a warning. The supported simple conditions are `true`, `false`, `success()`, `failure()`, `always()`, and `cancelled()`; unknown expressions or conditions are noted and skipped rather than evaluated (and make the run partial).

## Deliberate v1 limits

- Matrix jobs are skipped; matrix values are not expanded. Job-level `if:`, `container:` and `services:` are not read.
- `actions/checkout` is a no-op because the working tree is already present. Other `uses:` actions are skipped; third-party actions are not downloaded or executed.
- `GITHUB_ENV` accepts plain `NAME=value` lines; the multiline delimiter form is not supported.
- This runs scripts directly on your Mac, without a VM or container. Only test repositories and scripts you trust. Do not expect the result to exactly match GitHub's hosted runner image or security boundary.
- This is a small subset of Actions syntax, not a general-purpose Actions interpreter. Recheck important behavior in your actual CI environment.

Per-step and per-job `timeout-minutes` are honored, with a 30-minute default per step. Cancelling the CLI with Ctrl-C or pressing **Cancel** in the app terminates the active child process.

---

Source: https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/benchmarks.md

# Benchmarks

`kinhin bench` measures, on this Mac, how fast every runtime boots, how fast representative workloads run inside
them, how fast every toolchain in the [catalog](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/toolchains.md) installs and builds, and how long a
[demo video](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/videos-for-your-project.md) takes to render. It writes a
machine-readable report and removes everything it created. The same runs are available in the app under
**Advanced → Benchmarks**.

Use it to answer questions like _which runtime boots fastest here_, _what does Xcode cost on this machine_, _is my
disk the bottleneck_, or _how long will a fresh image take to bake_ — and to compare a change (a new image, a
different VM size, `tart_softnet`) before and after.

```sh
kinhin bench                         # boot, casual, xcode and large; minutes
kinhin bench boot --thorough         # 3 boot iterations per runtime, with min/median/max
kinhin bench xcode --project ~/src/MyApp
kinhin bench toolchains              # verify + a tiny build of every catalog tool (minutes)
kinhin bench toolchains --thorough --toolchains node,go,rust   # time the cold install too
kinhin bench video                   # time a short video build in a container runtime
kinhin bench --json > bench.json     # the report, on stdout only
```

## The suites

| Suite        | What it measures                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `boot`       | One row per runtime. Tart: `clone`, `boot-to-IP`, `IP-to-SSH-ready`, the cold total, and a warm stop/start. Containers: `start` and `exec-ready`. Host: `spawn` and `ready`. |
| `casual`     | One shared guest: per-exec overhead, a file tree (create, tar+gzip, untar, checksum), `git` commit of hundreds of files, and a `swift build` of a small generated package. |
| `xcode`      | `xcodebuild` clean and incremental builds of a generated multi-file Swift package, or of your checkout with `--project`. Skipped when the guest has no Xcode. |
| `large`      | Multi-gigabyte disk write, read and checksum, multi-core gzip throughput, and (with `--network`) a timed shallow `git clone`.                              |
| `toolchains` | One row per catalog tool and stack, per platform: cold install, verify, and a small offline workload. Opt-in: a thorough pass over the whole catalog takes tens of minutes (see [How long it takes](#how-long-it-takes)). |
| `video`      | A short generated video built with the [video pipeline](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/videos-for-your-project.md) in Apple `container` or Docker: the image pull (only when the image is missing), a `clean-build`, a `cached-build` that reuses the render cache, and with `--thorough` a `full-build` at full quality. Opt-in; skipped when no container runtime is running. |

`--quick` (the default) uses one boot iteration and small payloads. `--thorough` uses three iterations and larger
payloads (still capped at 4 GB), and makes the toolchains suite time the cold install.

Every suite names the runtime and guest platform it measured, so two runs compare across runtimes. Boot covers every
runtime whose prerequisites are healthy on this Mac, configured or not; a runtime that cannot run appears as
`skipped` with the reason (and `host` appears as skipped until you pass `--include-host`).

### Reading the numbers

- Timing is taken on the host around each command, so each step includes one command round trip. The
  `exec-overhead` step in `casual` is that round trip alone; subtract it when a step is short.
- Docker with `linux/amd64` runs under emulation and is much slower than `linux/arm64`. Thorough boot runs add a
  separate `linux/amd64` row when an amd64 image is on this Mac.
- `disk-read` can be served from the guest's page cache; read it as a ceiling.
- A toolchain row marked `preinstalled` was already in the image, so no install was timed. A quick run never installs:
  a tool the image lacks reads `skipped`.
- Tools with no meaningful offline workload (`playwright`, `cypress`, `fastlane`, `netlify-cli`, `k9s`, `pulumi`,
  `vault`, …) are verify-only and say why.

## Example results

Measured on a MacBook with an **Apple M1 Max, 10 cores and 64 GB of RAM**, macOS 27 with Xcode 27.0. Tart VMs had
4 vCPUs and 8 GB (with `tart_softnet: true`), Apple container 1 vCPU and 4 GB, Docker 2 vCPUs and 4 GB, all
`linux/arm64`. Unless noted these are `--quick` runs, so each number is a single sample. Your Mac, image and load will
differ: use them to see the shape of the report, not as a promise.

**Boot** (`kinhin bench boot`, thorough, 2 iterations for Tart):

| Runtime         | Phase                        | Median  |
| --------------- | ---------------------------- | ------- |
| Tart (macOS VM) | `clone`                      | 74 ms   |
|                 | `boot-to-IP`                 | 1.1 s   |
|                 | `IP-to-SSH-ready`            | 30.9 s  |
|                 | `cold-boot-total`            | 32.0 s  |
|                 | `warm-stop` / `warm-boot`    | 0.5 s / 10.6 s |
| Apple container | `start` / `exec-ready`       | 2.1 s / 112 ms |
| Docker          | `start` / `exec-ready`       | 268 ms / 102 ms |

The Tart `IP-to-SSH-ready` figure includes the 30 s window kinhin spends trying to pin the guest's SSH host key
through the guest agent; the near-identical 31 s in both iterations suggests this test image's guest agent did not answer, so the
full window elapsed before the connection was made (see [Security](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/security.md)).

**Casual, Xcode and Large** (Tart macOS VM versus a Docker container; `swift build` and Xcode need the macOS guest):

| Step                 | Tart (macOS) | Docker (Linux) |
| -------------------- | ------------ | -------------- |
| `exec-overhead`      | 161 ms       | 64 ms          |
| `file-create`        | 237 MB/s     | 647 MB/s       |
| `tar-gzip`           | 38.9 MB/s    | 42.9 MB/s      |
| `untar`              | 325 MB/s     | 193 MB/s       |
| `checksum`           | 151 MB/s     | 224 MB/s       |
| `git-commit`         | 296 ms       | 109 ms         |
| `swift-build`        | 16.5 s       | skipped (no Swift in the image) |
| Xcode `clean-build`  | 13.1 s       | n/a            |
| Xcode `incremental-build` | 3.2 s   | n/a            |
| `disk-write`         | 750 MB/s     | 569 MB/s       |
| `disk-read` (cached) | 2.9 GB/s     | 2.7 GB/s       |
| `cpu-gzip`           | 163 MB/s     | 53 MB/s        |
| `git-clone` (`--network`, shallow) | not run | 1.0 s |

**Toolchains** (`kinhin bench toolchains --thorough`, one fresh Docker container per tool, cold install with no shared
cache):

| Tool       | Install | Workload                    |
| ---------- | ------- | --------------------------- |
| `typescript` | 4.7 s | `tsc`, 318 ms (node already present) |
| `bun`      | 11.6 s  | script, 132 ms              |
| `just`     | 11.5 s  | `just`, 80 ms               |
| `helm`     | 11.5 s  | `helm create` + `template`, 123 ms |
| `terraform` | 12.3 s | `validate`, 121 ms          |
| `node`     | 13.8 s  | script, 101 ms              |
| `go`       | 14.2 s  | `go build`, 3.6 s           |
| `dotnet`   | 16.5 s  | `dotnet new` + `build`, 6.5 s |
| `python`   | 18.0 s  | script, 252 ms              |
| `java`     | 22.0 s  | `javac` + `java`, 487 ms    |
| `zig`      | 24.5 s  | `zig run`, 8.6 s            |
| `julia`    | 27.0 s  | script, 309 ms              |
| `maven`    | 43.3 s  | `mvn validate`, 966 ms      |

The same run reported tools that did not install in that container image as `failed` rows with the installer's output
(`elixir` needs `erl`, `lua` needs a C toolchain to build, `swift` failed extracting its archive), and `cmake` and `rust`
as verify-only because the image has no C compiler. That is the point of the table: it doubles as an install check.

## How long it takes

Measured on the M1 Max above (fast home connection, nothing else running):

| Run                                                                  | Time          |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| `kinhin bench boot --runtime docker,appleContainer`                  | about 4 s     |
| `kinhin bench casual large --runtime docker` (with `--network`)      | about 15 s    |
| `kinhin bench casual xcode large --runtime tart`                     | about 1.5 min |
| `kinhin bench boot --runtime tart --thorough --iterations 2`         | about 1.5 min |
| `kinhin bench toolchains --thorough --all-toolchains`, macOS (4 category VMs, 66 rows) | about 15 min  |
| the same, Linux on Apple container (one container per tool, 65 rows) | about 25 min  |
| `kinhin bench toolchains` (quick: verify + workload, nothing installed) | minutes     |
| `kinhin bench video` (image already pulled)                          | a few minutes; the first run also pulls the roughly 1 GB image |

The toolchains pass is dominated by downloads, so a slow connection can multiply it. The app and `bench_status` report
elapsed time and the current step while it runs.

## What has been tested

Honest status of this feature, as of the first complete implementation.

**Tested by the automated suite** (`swift test`, no VMs or network): the runner against the shared fakes (boot phases,
every suite's steps, cleanup on success, failure and cancel, fleet pause/resume/drain, the stray sweep, preflight
errors), the report and history store, the RPC handler and registry, the CLI parser and daemon polling, the app model,
the toolchain coverage invariants (every catalog tool and stack, on every platform it claims, has a plan and a
workload or a skip reason), and the stdin-isolating script wrapper against a real `bash`. A ThreadSanitizer run over
these tests found no races.

**Tested for real**, on an Apple M1 Max (64 GB), against real runtimes:

- **Tart macOS VM** (a 73 GB Xcode 27 image): `boot` (cold and warm, 2 iterations), `casual`, `xcode` (generated
  package and `--project` with a real Swift package), `large`, and the full toolchain catalog, installed cold (66 rows, none failed, 15 min).
- **Apple container** (`kinhin-ci-linux`): `boot` and the full toolchain catalog, installed cold. The last complete
  run predates two late fixes (stdin isolation, the gem path); a final full rerun was interrupted, and the affected
  entries (`fastlane`, `gcloud`, `swift`, `lua`, `elixir`) were re-run individually and pass.
- **Docker** (`kinhin-ci-linux`): `boot`, `casual`, `large` including `--network` (a real shallow clone), and about
  45 catalog tools installed cold.
- Cleanup was checked after each run: no `kinhin-bench-*` VM or container remained.
- The daemon methods (`bench_start`, `bench_status`, `bench_cancel`, including a cancelled run) over a real unix
  socket served by `RPCServer` with a throwaway engine.
- The Benchmarks view was rendered to an image from a real report to check its layout.

**Not tested yet:**

- Running through an actual `kinhin daemon` process (it would start the fleet, so the RPC path was exercised with a
  throwaway engine on a real socket instead).
- The app as a running window: clicking **Run…**, the confirmation dialog, live progress while a run goes, and the
  Fleet tab card. The model is unit-tested and the view renders, but nobody has used it end to end.
- Pausing a real fleet that has live, busy VMs (the pause, drain and resume logic is covered only with fakes), and the
  interactive confirmation prompt on a terminal.
- `--include-host` against the real host runtime (only a faked shell).
- The `linux/amd64` emulation pass on Docker, and a Docker run of the _whole_ catalog (about 45 tools were run; the
  Docker VM here was nearly out of disk, so `swift` was reported `skipped`, which is the intended behaviour).
- Tart Linux guests, thorough runs with more than two boot iterations, `--project` with an `.xcodeproj` or
  `.xcworkspace` (only a bare Swift package was built), and Intel Macs or other Xcode versions.

## How results are judged

- Entries that need build tools the base image lacks (a C toolchain for `lua`, `rust` and `cmake`, Python for
  `gcloud`, shared libraries for `swift`, Erlang for `elixir`, a modern Ruby and the gem `bin` directory for
  `fastlane`, the Flutter SDK step for `flutter`) get them as untimed prerequisites, so the run measures the tool and
  not the base image.
- An install that dies because the guest ran out of disk is reported `skipped` with the free space, not `failed`.
- A Tart VM that never gets a network lease gets one retry with a fresh VM.

## Flags

| Flag                              | Meaning                                                                                  |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `boot casual xcode large toolchains video` | Which suites to run (default: the first four).                                  |
| `--quick` / `--thorough`          | Payload sizes and iterations.                                                            |
| `--iterations N`                  | Boot iterations, 1 to 10.                                                                |
| `--runtime tart,docker,…`         | Only these runtimes (`tart`, `appleContainer`, `docker`, `host`, `all`).                 |
| `--toolchains ID,…`               | Scope the toolchains suite to these tools or stacks.                                     |
| `--all-toolchains`                | Cover the whole catalog (required for a thorough run that is not scoped).                |
| `--include-host`                  | Also benchmark the unisolated host runtime — see below.                                  |
| `--network URL`                   | Time a shallow `git clone` of an `https://`, `ssh://` or `git://` URL inside the guest.  |
| `--project PATH`                  | Copy a checkout into the macOS guest and build it with `xcodebuild`.                     |
| `--yes`                           | Agree to pause a running fleet without asking.                                           |
| `--force`                         | Do not wait for busy fleet VMs to finish before measuring.                               |
| `--keep`                          | Keep the host scratch directory (for debugging).                                         |
| `--json`                          | Print the report as the one JSON document on stdout; progress is silenced.               |

Exit codes follow the usual rule: 0 when every suite ran or was skipped, 1 when a suite or a toolchain
row failed, 2 for a bad command line, 4 when a benchmark could not run at all (a runtime or image is missing, not enough
free disk, the fleet would not drain).

## What it creates, and what it removes

**Created during the run, removed afterwards — also when the run fails or is cancelled:**

- Tart VMs and containers named `kinhin-bench-*`, cloned from your configured image. They are stopped and deleted, and
  their pinned SSH host keys are dropped.
- A `kinhin-bench/` directory inside each guest. (Deleting the guest discards it anyway.)
- A host scratch directory, `~/Library/Application Support/Kinhin/bench/<run-id>/`, holding generated sources, the
  `--project` archive and the `video` suite's throwaway repository, its rendered output and render cache. Removed whole
  unless `--keep`. Your own `.kinhin/videos/` folders are never touched.

**Kept:** the report, `results-<timestamp>-<id>.json` in `~/Library/Application Support/Kinhin/bench/`, newest 20.
Reports hold no credentials. The base image, the config file, the Keychain and the toolchain cache are never touched.

A crashed run can leave a `kinhin-bench-*` VM behind. The next `kinhin bench` sweeps it up before it starts, and
`kinhin cleanup` lists it with the other leftover VMs.

## The fleet is paused while it runs

A benchmark needs the Mac to itself, so a running fleet is held while it measures (a `video`-only run builds in a
container on the host, uses no VM and leaves the fleet alone):

1. If the fleet has live VMs, the CLI asks first (`--yes` agrees up front; a script that is not attached to a terminal
   must pass it). The app shows a confirmation dialog.
2. New spawns are paused and busy VMs are given up to ten minutes to finish their jobs (`--force` skips the wait).
3. The fleet is resumed when the run ends, including on failure or Ctrl-C. A fleet that was already paused is left
   paused.

With a daemon running, the daemon performs the run and pauses itself (the CLI polls for progress; Ctrl-C cancels the
run there too). With no daemon, the CLI runs the benchmark in its own process.

## Safety

- **No secrets.** A benchmark never reads the Keychain, mints a registration token or registers a runner, so no
  credential reaches a bench VM, a script or a report.
- **Same guest access as runners.** Bench guests are reached the way runner VMs are: kinhin's guest key, a per-VM
  pinned host key, and the image's hardened SSH. Bench VMs boot with your `tart_softnet` setting.
- **Bounded input.** `--project` is copied into the guest (never mounted) with relative-only archive extraction and
  is capped at 128 MB after excluding `.git`, `.build` and `node_modules`. `--network` accepts only git URL schemes
  and clones inside the disposable guest. Generated scripts quote every interpolated value, and nothing is ever
  piped from the network into a shell.
- **Offline toolchain workloads.** Workloads build generated sources only. Cloud CLIs run local flags, never live
  services.
- **Host mode is consent-gated.** `--include-host` mirrors the consent rule for host routes: the host runtime has no
  isolation, so it only runs when you ask, in a scrubbed scratch directory.
- **Limits.** Payload and iteration sizes are capped whatever the flags say, free disk is checked first, every command
  has a timeout, and cancelling tears everything down.

## From the app

**Advanced → Benchmarks** has a toggle per suite, a Quick/Thorough picker and a **Run…** button that confirms the
fleet pause. While a run is going it shows live progress, then the cross-runtime boot comparison, each suite's steps,
a sortable toolchains table (skip reasons inline) and the history of earlier reports. The Fleet tab has a card that
opens it. The app polls the run every two seconds, so closing the window does not stop it; reopening the section
re-attaches.

## Under the hood

`bench_start`, `bench_status` and `bench_cancel` are daemon RPC methods (see [architecture](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/architecture.md)): a run
outlives an RPC deadline, so the daemon starts it detached and clients poll its status. The measuring is
`BenchmarkRunner` in `Sources/KinhinKit/Benchmarks/`.

---

Source: https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane-tutorial.md

# Tutorial: your first TestFlight or Play internal build

This walks through a first release from a clean start: scaffold the project, set up the credentials once, run a `beta`
lane by hand, then run it from CI. It takes about an hour the first time, most of it waiting on Apple and Google.

[← Back to mobile releases](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane.md) · [Credentials](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-credentials.md) · [Troubleshooting](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane-troubleshooting.md)

## What you need

- A Mac with [kinhin installed](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/install.md) (`kinhin` on your PATH), Xcode, and Ruby 3.2 or newer. The macOS system Ruby (2.6) is too
  old. Install Ruby 3.3 with Homebrew (`brew install ruby@3.3`) or rbenv.
- For iOS: an Apple Developer Program membership. The **Account Holder** requests API access, and an **Account Holder** or **Admin** creates the team key.
- For Android: a Google Play Console developer account, and a Google Cloud project you can create a service account in.
- A repository for the app on any supported forge (GitHub, Gitea, Forgejo, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps or Buildkite), with a runner that has the `kinhin-xcode` label.

Your app already builds locally. Check that first: `flutter build`, `npx react-native run-ios`, or Xcode and Android
Studio for native apps.

## 1. Scaffold the project

From anywhere, point `kinhin mobile init` at the project folder:

```bash
kinhin mobile init --dry-run ~/code/my-app   # see what would be written
kinhin mobile init ~/code/my-app
```

It detects the framework. Flutter and React Native get fastlane in `ios/` and `android/`; a native app gets it at its root;
an Expo app gets `eas.json` only, unless you run `npx expo prebuild` first (see the [reference](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane.md#expo)).
It writes a `Gemfile` that pins fastlane, the lanes, and a release pipeline for your CI system. kinhin picks the system from
your `origin` remote, or from `--ci github|gitea|forgejo|gitlab|bitbucket|azure|buildkite`:

| Your forge | Pipeline file | Runner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub | `.github/workflows/mobile-release.yml` | `runs-on: [self-hosted, kinhin-xcode]` |
| Gitea, Forgejo | `.gitea/workflows/mobile-release.yml`, `.forgejo/workflows/mobile-release.yml` | `runs-on: [kinhin-xcode]` |
| GitLab | `.gitlab/mobile-release.yml`, included from `.gitlab-ci.yml` | `tags: [kinhin-xcode]` |
| Bitbucket | `bitbucket-pipelines.yml` (custom pipeline) | `runs-on: [self.hosted, macos, kinhin-xcode]` |
| Azure DevOps | `.azure-pipelines/mobile-release.yml` | pool `kinhin` |
| Buildkite | `.buildkite/mobile-release.yml` | queue `kinhin` |

Every non-GitHub system also gets `.kinhin/mobile-release.sh`, which holds the release steps. Existing files are kept, so you
can run it again safely. The [reference](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane.md#other-ci-systems) has the details.

Install the gems and list the lanes, from the folder that holds `fastlane/`:

```bash
cd ~/code/my-app/ios        # Flutter and React Native; a native app stays at its root
bundle install
bundle exec fastlane lanes
```

You should see `ios beta` and `ios release` (and `android beta` and `android build` in the Android folder). Commit the
scaffolded files before going on.

## 2. Create the App Store Connect API key (iOS)

App Store Connect uses an API key instead of your Apple ID password. In App Store Connect, open **Users and Access**,
then **Integrations**, then **App Store Connect API**, and request access if you have not yet (only the Account Holder can).
Create a **Team** key, and download the `.p8` file. Apple's page says API keys "can only be downloaded once". Apple's page does not list which roles can upload builds, so confirm the key works with a first upload.

Note the **Key ID** and the **Issuer ID**. You will store the `.p8` contents as a secret in step 4. The details are in
[credentials](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-credentials.md#app-store-connect-api-key).

## 3. Set up code signing with match (iOS)

`match` keeps your signing certificates and profiles in a private, encrypted git repository, so CI can use them without
you copying certificates by hand.

1. Create an empty private repository for certificates on any git host, for example `my-org/certificates`.
2. Choose a passphrase for it and keep it safe. It becomes `MATCH_PASSWORD`.
3. Run `match` once from your own Mac, not on CI, to create the certificates and profiles:

```bash
cd ~/code/my-app/ios
MATCH_GIT_URL=git@git.example.com:my-org/certificates.git MATCH_PASSWORD='your passphrase' \
  APP_IDENTIFIER=com.example.myapp APPLE_TEAM_ID=ABCDE12345 \
  MATCH_READONLY=false bundle exec fastlane match appstore
```

`match` asks for the passphrase, unless `MATCH_PASSWORD` is set, which avoids the prompt. Afterwards the repository holds the encrypted certificates. CI runs `match`
readonly, so it never creates or changes them.

## 4. Add the secrets

Add the secrets listed in the header of the pipeline file kinhin wrote. Where you add them depends on the forge:

| Forge | Where |
| --- | --- |
| GitHub | **Settings** > **Secrets and variables** > **Actions** |
| Gitea, Forgejo | Repository **Settings** > **Actions** > **Secrets** |
| GitLab | **Settings** > **CI/CD** > **Variables** (mask them; protect them for protected branches) |
| Bitbucket | **Repository settings** > **Pipelines** > **Repository variables** (secured) |
| Azure DevOps | **Pipelines** > the pipeline > **Variables** (keep this value secret) |
| Buildkite | the agent environment or a secrets manager; Buildkite has no secret store of its own |

For iOS you need `ASC_KEY_ID`, `ASC_ISSUER_ID`, `ASC_KEY_P8`,
`MATCH_GIT_URL`, `MATCH_PASSWORD`, `APPLE_TEAM_ID`, `APP_IDENTIFIER` and `IOS_SCHEME`. Each one is explained in
[credentials](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-credentials.md).

`IOS_SCHEME` is the Xcode scheme to build. For Flutter it is `Runner`, which is the default when the secret is empty.

## 5. Set up Android (optional, same steps)

1. Create an upload keystore once, and keep the file and its passwords somewhere safe:

```bash
keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore upload.keystore -alias upload -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
```

2. Store it base64-encoded, as `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_BASE64`. On macOS: `base64 -i upload.keystore | pbcopy`.
3. Create a Google Cloud service account, enable the Google Play Developer API for it, and invite it in Play Console with
   **Release apps to testing tracks** permission for your app. Store its JSON key as `PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON`.

The full steps are in [credentials](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-credentials.md#google-play-service-account).

The app must exist in Play Console before the first upload. Create it there, with the package name you put in
`ANDROID_PACKAGE_NAME`. The first upload is made by hand in Play Console, as the fastlane supply docs say. The lanes can upload after that.

## 6. Run a beta locally first

Before CI, run the lanes on your Mac. The lanes read the same variables as CI, but the API key and the keystore are
files, so point to them rather than pasting their contents. Keep the secret values out of shell history by putting them
in a file you do not commit, such as `~/.config/my-app/release.env`, and loading it with `set -a; source` for the session:

```bash
cd ~/code/my-app/ios
export ASC_KEY_ID=... ASC_ISSUER_ID=... APP_IDENTIFIER=com.example.myapp APPLE_TEAM_ID=ABCDE12345
export ASC_KEY_FILEPATH=~/keys/AuthKey_XXXX.p8     # the .p8 file, not its contents
export MATCH_GIT_URL=git@git.example.com:my-org/certificates.git MATCH_PASSWORD=...
bundle exec fastlane beta
```

For Android, set `PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON` to the JSON file's contents (for example `$(cat ~/keys/play.json)`), and set
`ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PATH` to the keystore file with its passwords and alias. CI does the same through the workflow.

A successful run uploads the build to TestFlight. Apple then processes it for a few minutes before it appears there.
Android works the same way, from the `android` folder: `bundle exec fastlane android beta` uploads to the internal track.
If you only want to check that the Android bundle builds and is signed, run `bundle exec fastlane android build`, which
does not upload.

## 7. Run it from CI

Start the `mobile-release` pipeline by hand and pick `beta` for the lane:

| Forge | How |
| --- | --- |
| GitHub, Gitea, Forgejo | **Actions** > **mobile-release** > **Run workflow** |
| GitLab | **Build** > **Pipelines** > **Run pipeline**, with `MOBILE_LANE` set to `beta` |
| Bitbucket | **Pipelines** > **Run pipeline** > custom: `mobile-release` |
| Azure DevOps | run the pipeline made from `.azure-pipelines/mobile-release.yml` |
| Buildkite | build a pipeline whose steps upload `.buildkite/mobile-release.yml` |

On GitHub the job installs Ruby, and for Flutter and React Native the framework tools first, then runs the lane. On the
other systems `.kinhin/mobile-release.sh` does this, using the toolchains on your runner image. If it fails, the
first error is in the log of the failing step. The [troubleshooting](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane-troubleshooting.md) page lists the
failures we have seen, with what to do about each.

Use `release` only after a `beta` build has finished processing and you have checked it in TestFlight. The `release`
lane uploads the build to App Store Connect without submitting it for review.

## Where to go next

- The [reference](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane.md) covers each framework, the monorepo layout and the Expo route.
- Add a second lane for production, or wire the `release` lane to a tag, once beta is working for you.

---

Source: https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane.md

# Mobile releases with fastlane

This is opt-in. kinhin's runners, configuration and commands work exactly as before unless you run `kinhin mobile init`
in a project. Running it only adds files to that project: fastlane lanes, a `Gemfile`, and a CI workflow. kinhin's own
config is not read or changed by it.

Scaffold fastlane into an iOS, Android, Flutter, React Native, Expo, Capacitor, Kotlin Multiplatform or .NET MAUI project, and run store uploads from a kinhin
runner. `kinhin mobile init` writes the lanes, a pinned Gemfile and a manual release workflow. Nothing is uploaded until you
trigger the workflow.

[← Back to toolchains](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/toolchains.md)

## Quick start

Install kinhin, then run this from anywhere, with the project folder as the argument. The [tutorial](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane-tutorial.md) walks through a first build end to end, the [credentials](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-credentials.md) page covers each secret, and [store screenshots](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-screenshots.md) covers the `screenshots` lane:

```bash
kinhin mobile init /path/to/your/app
```

It detects the framework, then writes only the files that are missing:

| Project | Detected by | Writes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flutter | `pubspec.yaml` | `Gemfile`, `ios/fastlane/`, `android/fastlane/`, `.github/workflows/mobile-release.yml` |
| React Native (bare) | `"react-native"` in `package.json` | same as Flutter |
| Capacitor / Ionic | `"@capacitor/core"` in `package.json` | same as Flutter. Each platform's CI job runs `npm run build` and `npx cap sync`. |
| Kotlin Multiplatform | `iosApp/`, Gradle settings, and the multiplatform plugin in a build file | `iosApp/fastlane/`, `androidApp/fastlane/`, workflow. The Xcode build phase builds the shared framework. |
| .NET MAUI | a `.csproj` with `<UseMaui>true</UseMaui>` (root or one folder down) | `ios/fastlane/`, `android/fastlane/`, workflow. `dotnet publish` builds and signs the artifacts. |
| Expo | `"expo"` in `package.json` | `eas.json` only. Expo uses EAS by default (see [Expo](#expo)). |
| Native iOS | `ios/` or `*.xcodeproj` / `*.xcworkspace` | `Gemfile`, `fastlane/` (or `ios/fastlane/`), workflow |
| Native Android | `android/` or `settings.gradle(.kts)` | `Gemfile`, `fastlane/` (or `android/fastlane/`), workflow |

Flags:

- `--framework ios|android|flutter|react-native|expo|capacitor|kmp|maui|native` overrides detection.
- `--ci github|gitea|forgejo|gitlab|bitbucket|azure|buildkite` picks the CI system the release pipeline is written for.
  By default it is detected: a `.buildkite/` folder or Azure Pipelines file, then the host of the `origin` remote, then the
  repository's other CI files, else GitHub. See [Other CI systems](#other-ci-systems).
- `--force` overwrites files that already exist.
- `--dry-run` prints what would be written.

Then, in the project:

```bash
bundle install
# Run from the folder that holds fastlane/: ios/ or android/ for Flutter and React Native,
# the project root for a native project with its project file at the root.
cd ios && bundle exec fastlane lanes
cd ../android && bundle exec fastlane lanes
```

## Lanes

| Platform | Lane | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| iOS | `beta` | `match` (readonly) → `build_app` (App Store export; `IPA_PATH` or `dotnet publish` for MAUI replaces it) → `upload_to_testflight` |
| iOS | `release` | `upload_to_app_store` with metadata and screenshots skipped; not submitted for review |
| iOS | `screenshots` | `snapshot` (UI tests on a simulator) → optional `frameit` (`FRAME_SCREENSHOTS=1`) → optional upload (`UPLOAD_SCREENSHOTS=1`). See [store screenshots](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-screenshots.md). |
| Android | `screenshots` | `screengrab` (instrumented tests on an emulator) → optional upload (`UPLOAD_SCREENSHOTS=1`). See [store screenshots](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-screenshots.md). |
| Android | `beta` | `gradle` builds a release AAB (or uses `AAB_PATH`; `dotnet publish` for MAUI) → `upload_to_play_store` to the internal track |

The templates use the documented fastlane interfaces: `app_store_connect_api_key` with `match`, `pilot` and `deliver`
with API key auth, and `supply` with a service account JSON. See the sources at the end.

## Secrets

Nothing secret is committed. Create these as repository secrets, and the workflow maps them into the lanes:

| Secret | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| `ASC_KEY_ID`, `ASC_ISSUER_ID`, `ASC_KEY_P8` | App Store Connect API key. The `.p8` file is written to a temp path in the job, then deleted. |
| `MATCH_GIT_URL`, `MATCH_PASSWORD` | Encrypted certificates repo for `match` (readonly on CI) |
| `APPLE_TEAM_ID`, `APP_IDENTIFIER`, `IOS_SCHEME` | iOS app and build settings |
| `PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON` | Google Play Developer API (`supply`) |
| `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_BASE64`, `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD`, `ANDROID_KEY_ALIAS`, `ANDROID_KEY_PASSWORD` | Upload keystore, passed to Gradle as `android.injected.signing.*` |
| `ANDROID_PACKAGE_NAME` | Play package name |
| `MAUI_CODESIGN_KEY`, `MAUI_PROVISIONING_PROFILE` (variables, not secrets) | .NET MAUI iOS signing: the identity and profile name that `match` installed. See [.NET MAUI](#net-maui). |

## Lane environment variables

The lanes read these from the environment. The CI jobs set them; set them yourself for a local run.

| Variable | Lane | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `IOS_PROJECT`, `IOS_WORKSPACE` | iOS | Xcode project or workspace, when it is not at the default place. Passed to `build_app` and `snapshot`. |
| `IPA_PATH` | iOS | An IPA that another step already built and signed. The lane skips `build_app` and uploads it. |
| `IPA_MAX_AGE_HOURS` | iOS | How old `IPA_PATH` may be (default 24). An older IPA is refused. |
| `MAUI_PROJECT` | iOS, Android | The .NET MAUI `.csproj`, relative to the app folder. The lane runs `dotnet publish` instead of Gradle or `build_app`. |
| `ANDROID_GRADLE_DIR` | Android | The Gradle root, relative to the Android folder (Kotlin Multiplatform: `..`). |
| `ANDROID_GRADLE_MODULE` | Android | The module that holds the app (default `app`). Kotlin Multiplatform: `androidApp`. |
| `AAB_PATH` | Android | A bundle that another step already built. The lane skips Gradle. |

Create the App Store Connect API key once: the Account Holder requests API access under **Integrations**, then an Account
Holder or Admin creates a team key. You can download the `.p8` once only. Team keys cover all apps and cannot be limited per app.

## Runner

The workflow asks for `runs-on: [self-hosted, kinhin-xcode]`, the Xcode image label. If your pool uses another label,
change it in `.github/workflows/mobile-release.yml`. kinhin does not store any of these secrets.

**Versions as variables.** The toolchain versions are set in the workflow, but you can override them without editing it:
`DOTNET_VERSION` (MAUI's .NET SDK, default `10.0.x`) and `JAVA_VERSION` (the Java for the Android job; defaults to 21 for
Capacitor and 17 otherwise). Set them as repository variables to test a newer SDK or JDK. The Actions stay pinned to commit
SHAs, so a newer action needs its SHA updated in the templates.

**Ruby.** fastlane 2.241, which the `~> 2.240` pin resolves to, needs Ruby 3.2 or newer. The macOS system Ruby is 2.6, so the workflow installs Homebrew's Ruby on the runner before `bundle install`. Homebrew's Ruby is newer than 3.2 and ships bundler. Locally, use Ruby 3.2 or newer (for example `rbenv` or Homebrew's `ruby@3.3`).

## Other CI systems

GitHub gets the workflow described above. Every other system gets two files: `.kinhin/mobile-release.sh` in the app folder,
which holds the release steps as shell (the framework's setup, the signing files from secrets, `bundle install`, the lane),
and a small pipeline file that starts it by hand, targets the Xcode runner, passes the secrets as environment variables and
keeps the screenshots. The script takes the platform and lane: `bash .kinhin/mobile-release.sh ios beta`.

| `--ci` | Pipeline file | Runner | Start it from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gitea`, `forgejo` | `.gitea/workflows/mobile-release.yml`, `.forgejo/workflows/mobile-release.yml` | `runs-on: [kinhin-xcode]` | Actions > mobile-release > Run workflow |
| `gitlab` | `.gitlab/mobile-release.yml`, included from `.gitlab-ci.yml` | `tags: [kinhin-xcode]` | Build > Pipelines > Run pipeline (set `MOBILE_LANE`) |
| `bitbucket` | `bitbucket-pipelines.yml` (a custom pipeline) | `runs-on: [self.hosted, macos, kinhin-xcode]` | Pipelines > Run pipeline > custom: mobile-release |
| `azure` | `.azure-pipelines/mobile-release.yml` | the `kinhin` pool, `demands: [kinhin_xcode]` | a pipeline made from that file |
| `buildkite` | `.buildkite/mobile-release.yml` | `agents: { queue: kinhin }` | a pipeline whose steps upload that file |

kinhin never edits a pipeline file the repository already has. With an existing `.gitlab-ci.yml` it prints the `include:`
line to add; with an existing `bitbucket-pipelines.yml` it writes `bitbucket-pipelines.mobile-release.yml` beside it, for you
to copy the `mobile-release` entry from.

There are no setup actions outside GitHub, so the runner image supplies the tools: Ruby 3.2 or newer (the script installs
`ruby@3.3` with mise when the image has mise and an older Ruby), and Node, Flutter, Java or .NET as the app needs. Declare them
in the repository's `.kinhin/config.yml` ([toolchains](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/toolchains.md); `kinhin toolchains detect --write` proposes the list).
Gitea and Forgejo run `actions/checkout` and `actions/upload-artifact` (v3, the artifact protocol those servers implement) by
full GitHub URL, so the image also needs Node.js for those two actions.

## Framework notes

The generated CI jobs run the framework's own setup before the lanes, so a clean checkout builds without manual steps.
A monorepo app works too; see [Monorepos](#monorepos).

**Flutter.** The jobs install the Flutter SDK (`subosito/flutter-action`) and run `flutter pub get`, which also writes
`android/local.properties`. On iOS they run `flutter build ios --config-only --release` before CocoaPods, so the
generated Flutter config exists when the Xcode project is built. The Android lane then builds the signed bundle with
Gradle, using the same signing properties as the native projects, and finds it at `build/app/outputs/bundle/release/`.
Set `AAB_PATH` only when another step has already built a bundle; then Gradle is skipped. An IPA build needs a
distribution certificate, not a development one. The iOS deployment target must be 15.0 or higher for the Xcode 26
toolchain: `flutter create` still writes 13.0, which fails with "deployment target ... is set to 13.0". The `flutter_app`
example sets 15.0 in `ios/Runner.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj`.

**React Native (bare).** The jobs set up Node 22 and install dependencies before CocoaPods and Gradle run: `npm ci` when
there is a `package-lock.json`, `yarn install --frozen-lockfile` when there is a `yarn.lock`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`
when there is a `pnpm-lock.yaml`, and `npm install` otherwise.
No official fastlane guide exists for React Native. The layout follows fastlane's standard setup. The e2e checks the same
steps (npm, pod install, a simulator build and the signed Android bundle), but a real store upload is still unverified.
The Android build needs `ANDROID_HOME` on the runner, or an `android/local.properties` with `sdk.dir`.

**Native.** Works for projects with `ios/` and `android/` folders, or with the project files at the root.

## Capacitor and Ionic

Capacitor keeps its iOS project in `ios/App/App.xcodeproj`, one level below the fastlane folder. The CI job exports
`IOS_PROJECT=App/App.xcodeproj` for that, so the iOS lanes find the project. For a local run, set it yourself:

```bash
cd ios
IOS_PROJECT=App/App.xcodeproj bundle exec fastlane beta
```

Capacitor 8's Android library needs Java 21, so the Android job uses Java 21 for Capacitor projects (the other frameworks use
Java 17). Capacitor 8 resolves its iOS packages with Swift Package Manager, so there is no Podfile.

Capacitor generates `ios/App/App.xcodeproj`, and the kinhin repository ignores `*.xcodeproj` for its XcodeGen examples, so a
Capacitor project that lives in a kinhin repository needs an exception in its `.gitignore`. `examples/capacitor_app` shows it.

## Kotlin Multiplatform

Detected by an `iosApp/` folder, Gradle settings, and the multiplatform plugin in a build file (the root or `shared/`).
The Android module is `androidApp` under a Gradle root one folder above `androidApp/`. The CI jobs set
`ANDROID_GRADLE_DIR=..` and `ANDROID_GRADLE_MODULE=androidApp`, so the lanes build `:androidApp:bundle`. For a local run, set
them yourself. The iOS build runs the Xcode build phase, which calls `./gradlew :shared:embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode`.
Run Gradle with JDK 17 (JDK 26 fails with Kotlin), and export `JAVA_HOME` before a plain `./gradlew` run.

## .NET MAUI

Detected by a `.csproj` with `<UseMaui>true</UseMaui>` at the root or one folder down. The iOS build needs macOS and the
.NET 10 SDK with the MAUI workload (`dotnet workload install maui`). The CI job installs the SDK with `actions/setup-dotnet`,
but the Linux catalog entry still pins the apt `dotnet-sdk-8.0`, which cannot build MAUI for .NET 10. MAUI's iOS build runs
on macOS only.

fastlane signs nothing for MAUI. The lanes call `dotnet publish` with `MAUI_PROJECT` set to the `.csproj` (the CI jobs set it).
The iOS lane runs after `match`, so it can sign with the certificate match installed. Set `MAUI_CODESIGN_KEY` (the signing
identity) and `MAUI_PROVISIONING_PROFILE` (the profile name) as repository variables. The Android lane signs the AAB with the
upload keystore. Screenshots are not scaffolded for MAUI, because MAUI does not generate UI test projects.

## Expo

Expo's recommended path is EAS Build and EAS Submit. Expo local builds are supported, but Expo says the toolchain is
yours to provide (fastlane included), only one platform builds per run, and `eas.json`'s `fastlane` and `ndk` keys are
ignored in local builds. `kinhin mobile init` therefore writes only `eas.json` for Expo.

To use fastlane with Expo, create the native folders, then scaffold them as a React Native project:

```bash
npm install
npx expo prebuild --no-install   # creates ios/ and android/ (both platforms when no --platform is given)
kinhin mobile init --framework react-native .
```

The e2e runs this route: it builds the Android bundle through the lane with a signing keystore, and runs `pod install` and
a Release device build for iOS. Expo's own `--platform` flag takes one value, so leave it out to get both platforms.

Caveats to check before relying on this:

- EAS Submit uploads to TestFlight. The iOS `release` lane uploads a build to App Store Connect without submitting it for review.
- The docs do not say whether `eas-build-pre-install` hooks run in local builds. Test it before depending on it.

## Monorepos

`kinhin mobile init` writes the workflow to the git repository's own `.github/workflows/` (the only place GitHub reads
workflows from), with paths relative to that repository. For an app at `apps/mobile` in a monorepo, the jobs run
`working-directory: apps/mobile/ios` and the setup steps run in `apps/mobile`.
Run it from the app folder, or pass the path: `kinhin mobile init apps/mobile`. A project with no git repository above it
gets paths from its own root.

## Errors you may see

The full list, with the cause and the fix for each, is in the [troubleshooting page](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane-troubleshooting.md). The
most common ones:

| Message | Where | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `no iOS or Android project in ...; pass --framework` | `kinhin mobile init` | The folder has no detectable project. Pass `--framework`. |
| `no ios/ or android/ folder in ... for a flutter project` | `kinhin mobile init` | Run `flutter create` (or `react-native init`) first. |
| `Missing environment variables: ASC_KEY_ID, ...` | fastlane | Set the listed secrets. The lane stops before any store call. |
| `ASC_KEY_FILEPATH does not exist` | fastlane | The `.p8` was not written. Check the "Write App Store Connect API key" step. |
| `Keystore not found at ...` | fastlane | Check `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_BASE64` and the "Write upload keystore" step. |
| `No release AAB at ...` | fastlane | Gradle did not produce the bundle. Check `AAB_PATH` and the Gradle output. |
| `No IPA at ...`, `IPA at ... is older than N hours` | fastlane | `IPA_PATH` points at a missing or stale IPA. Rebuild it, or raise `IPA_MAX_AGE_HOURS`. |
| `dotnet publish wrote no IPA` / `no AAB` | fastlane | The MAUI build produced no artifact. Read the `dotnet publish` output above it. |
| `Cannot locate tasks that match ':androidApp:bundleRelease'` | fastlane | Kotlin Multiplatform: the Gradle task name is set by the lane. Check `ANDROID_GRADLE_MODULE`. |

The `MobileScaffoldTests` Swift tests cover the scaffolding logic. They run in `swift test`, which CI and `scripts/check.sh` both run.

## Verification

Two checks cover the integration:

- The `MobileScaffoldTests` Swift tests cover the scaffolding: detection, keep and force, dry run, monorepo paths and the
  error paths. They run in `swift test`, which `scripts/check.sh` and CI both run.
- `scripts/mobile-e2e.sh` runs against a clean copy of the committed examples. It checks the templates still generate
  the committed examples, runs `bundle install` and lists the lanes, checks the secret errors in an empty environment,
  lints the generated workflows with actionlint, and confirms every fastlane option the templates use exists.
  `--with-builds` adds the native, Flutter and React Native builds and the signed-bundle check. It needs Ruby 3.2+ (set
  `RUBY_BIN` if it is not on the usual path). Building the binary needs Swift; the builds need JDK 17, an Android SDK,
  Xcode, Flutter, XcodeGen, and `jarsigner` (part of the JDK). The React Native steps need npm and CocoaPods.

The e2e script does not upload anything and does not read credentials. The store and runner steps still need a real
project. The checklist in `docs/plans/mobile-fastlane-test-checklist.md` lists what is covered and what is not.

Run this checklist on a fixture project before you trust a release:

1. `kinhin mobile init --dry-run /path/to/app` lists what would be written.
2. `bundle install` succeeds with Ruby 3.2 or newer.
3. `bundle exec fastlane lanes` lists the lanes, run from each platform's folder (see Quick start).
4. Trigger `mobile-release` with `lane: beta` against a test app and confirm the TestFlight or internal track build.
5. Re-run `kinhin mobile init` and confirm existing files are kept.

## Sources

Checked 2026-10-11. The versions and dates below are what those pages showed.

- fastlane setup: [iOS](https://docs.fastlane.tools/getting-started/ios/setup/), [Android](https://docs.fastlane.tools/getting-started/android/setup/). fastlane 2.240.1 was the latest release seen on [GitHub](https://github.com/fastlane/fastlane/releases) (2026-09-15). The Gemfile pin `~> 2.240` should be rechecked on each update.
- Actions: [`match`](https://docs.fastlane.tools/actions/match/), [`pilot`](https://docs.fastlane.tools/actions/pilot/), [`deliver`](https://docs.fastlane.tools/actions/deliver/), [`gym`](https://docs.fastlane.tools/actions/gym/), [`supply`](https://docs.fastlane.tools/actions/supply/), [`gradle`](https://docs.fastlane.tools/actions/gradle/), [`app_store_connect_api_key`](https://docs.fastlane.tools/actions/app_store_connect_api_key/)
- CI: [fastlane with GitHub Actions](https://docs.fastlane.tools/best-practices/continuous-integration/github/)
- Flutter: [Continuous Delivery](https://docs.flutter.dev/deployment/cd)

# Mobile release credentials

Every secret the release workflow reads, where to get it, and what each one is for. None of them are stored by kinhin.
Store them as repository secrets (**Settings**, then **Secrets and variables**, then **Actions**). The workflow maps them
into the lanes, and each lane checks for the ones it needs before any store call.

[← Back to mobile releases](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane.md) · [Tutorial](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane-tutorial.md) · [Troubleshooting](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane-troubleshooting.md)

| Secret | Platform | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ASC_KEY_ID` | iOS | App Store Connect API key ID |
| `ASC_ISSUER_ID` | iOS | App Store Connect issuer ID |
| `ASC_KEY_P8` | iOS | Contents of the `.p8` key file |
| `MATCH_GIT_URL` | iOS | Git URL of the certificates repository |
| `MATCH_PASSWORD` | iOS | Passphrase that encrypts the certificates repository |
| `APPLE_TEAM_ID` | iOS | Developer Portal team ID |
| `APP_IDENTIFIER` | iOS | Bundle ID, for example `com.example.myapp` |
| `IOS_SCHEME` | iOS | Xcode scheme to build. Empty means the project's default (`Runner` for Flutter). |
| `ANDROID_PACKAGE_NAME` | Android | Application ID, for example `com.example.myapp` |
| `PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON` | Android | JSON key of the Google Play service account |
| `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_BASE64` | Android | Upload keystore, base64-encoded |
| `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD` | Android | Keystore password |
| `ANDROID_KEY_ALIAS` | Android | Alias of the upload key in the keystore |
| `ANDROID_KEY_PASSWORD` | Android | Password of the upload key |

## App Store Connect API key

The key lets fastlane upload builds without your Apple ID password.

1. In App Store Connect, open **Users and Access**, then **Integrations**, then **App Store Connect API**.
2. If the API has not been enabled for the team, the Account Holder must request access there first.
3. Choose **Generate API Key** (a **Team** key). Only the Account Holder or an Admin can create a team key, and each key is
   assigned a role. Apple's API page does not list which roles can upload builds, so confirm the key works with one upload
   before you rely on it. Team keys apply to every app in the team. Individual keys belong to one user.
4. Download the `.p8` file. Apple's page says API keys "can only be downloaded once": if you lose it, revoke the key and create another.
5. Copy the **Key ID** into `ASC_KEY_ID`, and the **Issuer ID** shown at the top of the page into `ASC_ISSUER_ID`.
6. Store the contents of the `.p8` file as `ASC_KEY_P8`. The workflow writes it to a temporary file during the job and
   deletes it afterwards. On macOS, `pbcopy < AuthKey_XXXX.p8` copies it.

Revoke a key you no longer use. Anyone with the `.p8` and the IDs can act with its role.

## Match: certificates and profiles

`match` keeps signing certificates and provisioning profiles in a git repository, encrypted with `MATCH_PASSWORD`.

1. Create an empty **private** repository for it, for example `my-org/certificates`.
2. Set `MATCH_GIT_URL` to its SSH or HTTPS URL. kinhin's `Matchfile` reads this variable; `match` itself takes the URL as
   `git_url`. The CI runner needs read access to the repository. `match` can authenticate with its `git_private_key`,
   `git_basic_authorization` or `git_bearer_authorization` options, which the templates do not set yet.
3. Choose `MATCH_PASSWORD`, and keep a copy somewhere safe. Without it the repository cannot be decrypted.
4. Create the certificates once from your own Mac: `MATCH_READONLY=false bundle exec fastlane match appstore`. After that the
   CI job runs `match` readonly and only reads them.

## Apple team and bundle ID

- `APPLE_TEAM_ID` is the 10-character team ID. It is in the **Membership details** section of your Apple Developer account page
  (developer.apple.com/account). Apple's help index does not document this location, so check it against your own account.
- `APP_IDENTIFIER` is the bundle ID, which must match the app in App Store Connect. Create the app there first, with the
  same bundle ID.

## Google Play service account

Play uploads use a service account that the Play Developer API trusts.

1. In Google Cloud, create a project, or use an existing one, and enable the **Google Play Android Developer API**.
2. Create a service account, and create a **JSON key** for it. Keep the file private.
3. In Play Console, open **Users and permissions**, invite the service account's email address, and grant it release
   permissions for your app. Google lists **Release apps to testing tracks** as the permission for testing-track releases.
   Its permissions page does not say which permission a service account needs, so confirm the upload works on your first try.
   Uploading to a testing track needs the permission above. The first upload of a new app is covered below.
4. Store the whole JSON file as `PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON`.

The first upload of a new app is made by hand in Play Console, as the fastlane supply docs say. Once the app exists and has
a release, the lanes can upload.

## Android upload keystore

Google Play App Signing holds the app's signing key. You sign uploads with an upload key, which is the keystore below.

```bash
keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore upload.keystore -alias upload -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
```

- `ANDROID_KEY_ALIAS` is the alias you chose (`upload` above).
- `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD` and `ANDROID_KEY_PASSWORD` are the passwords you entered.
- `ANDROID_KEYSTORE_BASE64` is the keystore, base64-encoded: `base64 -i upload.keystore | pbcopy` on macOS.

Back up the keystore and its passwords. If you lose the upload key, Google says you are not locked out. Request a reset in
Play Console, in the **Upload key certificate** section, after exporting the new key's certificate in PEM format.

## .NET MAUI signing

The iOS lane runs `dotnet publish` after `match`, so the certificate and profile must be in the keychain first. Use the
identity and profile that `match` installed. Set them as repository variables (not secrets; they are not sensitive):

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `MAUI_CODESIGN_KEY` | The signing identity, for example `Apple Distribution: Your Name (ABCDE12345)` |
| `MAUI_PROVISIONING_PROFILE` | The provisioning profile name that `match` installed, for example `match AppStore com.example.app` |

The Android lane signs the AAB with the same upload keystore as the Gradle projects (`ANDROID_KEYSTORE_BASE64` and the
other Android secrets above). Nothing else changes for MAUI.

## Checking a secret before a run

A lane names the missing variables and stops before any store call. For example, `fastlane ios beta` without
`ASC_KEY_ID` fails with `Missing environment variables: ASC_KEY_ID, ...`. A variable can be set but still wrong. Those
show up later, as an authentication or signing error, which the [troubleshooting](https://kinhin.dev/v0.0.1-beta-4/guide/mobile-fastlane-troubleshooting.md)
page covers.

## Sources

Checked against these pages. Where a page does not settle a point, the guide says so.

- Apple, App Store Connect API: <https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/get-started/app-store-connect-api/>
  (who requests access, which roles create team and individual keys, and that a private key can be downloaded only once).
- fastlane, `match`: <https://docs.fastlane.tools/actions/match/> (`MATCH_PASSWORD`, `readonly`, the CI recommendation, and
  `match appstore`).
- fastlane, `setup_ci`: <https://docs.fastlane.tools/actions/setup_ci/> (the temporary keychain and readonly on CI; iOS and macOS).
- fastlane, `supply`: <https://docs.fastlane.tools/actions/supply/> (`json_key_data`, and that a new app's first build is
  uploaded manually).
- Google, Play Developer API: <https://developers.google.com/android-publisher/getting_started> (service account, enabling
  the API, and inviting the service account in Play Console).
- Google, Play Console permissions: <https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9844686> (the
  **Release apps to testing tracks** permission).
- Google, Play App Signing upload key reset: <https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9842756>.
- fastlane 2.241.0 gem metadata: `required_ruby_version >= 3.2.0`, read with `gem spec fastlane -v 2.241.0`.

Not settled by these pages: the Apple role that can upload builds, the Team ID location (Apple's help index does not list it),
and the Play permission a service account needs for test-track uploads. Check each one in the console before you rely on it.
